KP integrability through the x−yx-y swap relation

A. Alexandrov Address: A. A.: Center for Geometry and Physics, Institute for Basic Science (IBS), Pohang 37673, Korea Email address: alex@ibs.re.kr , B. Bychkov Address: B. B.: Department of Mathematics, University of Haifa, Mount Carmel, 3498838, Haifa, Israel Email address: bbychkov@hse.ru , P. Dunin-Barkowski Address: P. D.-B.: Faculty of Mathematics, National Research University Higher School of Economics, Usacheva 6, 119048 Moscow, Russia; HSE–Skoltech International Laboratory of Representation Theory and Mathematical Physics, Skoltech, Bolshoy Boulevard 30 bld. 1, 121205 Moscow, Russia; and NRC “Kurchatov Institute” – ITEP, 117218 Moscow, Russia Email address: ptdunin@hse.ru , M. Kazarian Address: M. K.: Faculty of Mathematics, National Research University Higher School of Economics, Usacheva 6, 119048 Moscow, Russia; and Igor Krichever Center for Advanced Studies, Skoltech, Bolshoy Boulevard 30 bld. 1, 121205 Moscow, Russia Email address: kazarian@mccme.ru and S. Shadrin Address: S. S.: Korteweg-de Vries Institute for Mathematics, University of Amsterdam, Postbus 94248, 1090GE Amsterdam, The Netherlands Email address: S.Shadrin@uva.nl
Abstract.

We discuss a universal relation that we call the x−yx-y swap relation, which plays a prominent role in the theory of topological recursion, Hurwitz theory, and free probability theory. We describe in a very precise and detailed way the interaction of the x−yx-y swap relation and KP integrability. As an application, we prove a recent conjecture that relates some particular instances of topological recursion to the Mironov–Morozov–Semenoff matrix integrals.

Part I Formulations and results

1. Pre-introduction

This paper deals with the so-called x−yx-y swap relation as the main object of study. This relation, in its several different reincarnations, appears to be ubiquitous in various areas of mathematics [ABDBKS25, BCGFLS21, BGF20, BCDGF19, BDBKS23, BCGF24, Hoc23, Hoc24, Hoc23a]. We discuss in details the structure of this relation, representing it in several different ways, and prove that this relation preserves KP integrability as a general property of systems of differentials.

In order to present the results of the paper, we have decided to split them in three independent layers. Firstly, we just introduce in Part 1 of the Introduction (Section 2) in a precise but very rough way the main results that can be understood without going deeply into the structure of the x−yx-y swap relation and/or KP integrability. Then, in Part 2 of the Introduction (Section 3) we go deeper inside the structures related to KP integrability and formulate the results on their transformation rules under the x−yx-y swap relation. Finally, in Part 3 of the Introduction (Section 4) we present a system of internal constructions and equivalent reformulations of x−yx-y symmetry that all together fully revisit the x−yx-y swap relation and connect it to KP integrability. Importantly, these reformulations avoid the complicated combinatorics of sums over graphs which appear in the original formulation of the x−yx-y swap relation.

One of the basic principles that we formulate in this paper is the concept of KP integrability as a property of a system of symmetric meromorphic differentials {ωn(g)}g≥0,n≥1\{\omega^{(g)}_{n}\}_{g\geq 0,n\geq 1} that are all regular along the diagonal, except for the (g,n)=(0,2)(g,n)=(0,2) case. This principle is stated in Theorem 2.3 as an assertion that the KP integrability property does not depend on the point of expansion.

The main results of the paper are Theorem 2.8 that basically states that the x−yx-y swap relation preserves KP integrability; Theorem 3.13 that gives a Gaussian integral transformation for the corresponding Baker–Akhiezer kernels; and Theorem 4.3 that represents a deep structure behind the x−yx-y swap relation that is responsible for the transfer of integrability properties.

The main applications concern the questions of KP integrability in the theory of spectral curve topological recursion [EO09, BE13]: Theorem 2.9 resolves a conjecture in [AD25, CGFG23] that a particular instance of topological recursion reproduces the Mironov–Morozov–Semenoff matrix integral, and Theorem 3.19 describes a quite general situation when our theory provides an explicit description of the KP tau function associated to the correlation differentials of topological recursion. We also prove that in the context of topological recursion the KP integrability property requires that the spectral curve is rational, see Theorem 3.8.

Beyond applications in topological recursion we have a quite general statement on the particular representation as Gaussian integrals for the basis vectors that span the half-infinite planes (or, equivalently, points in the Sato–Wilson Grassmannian) corresponding to tau functions obtained by application of x−yx-y swap relation to the trivial case, see Corollary 3.16.

1.1. Notation

i\mathrm{i} denotes −1\sqrt{-1}. For a function f⁡(x)f(x) the expression ⌊x→a⁡f⁡(x)\mathop{\big\lfloor_{{x}\to{a}}}f(x) stands for f⁡(a)f(a). By ⟦n⟧\llbracket n\rrbracket we mean the set {1,…,n}\{1,\dots,n\}, and x⟦n⟧x_{\llbracket n\rrbracket} denotes the set of variables {x1,…,xn}\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\}.

1.2. Organization of the paper

Sections 2–4 form together an introduction, where we formulate our results as described above. We supply our statements with immediate proofs if they are sufficiently short and do not use involved computations with the Gaussian integrals (the latter integrals are the main technique we use in this paper). In Section 5 we prove the results that concern the semi-classical limit of the corresponding KP tau functions (which are, in particular, necessary to describe the possible form of the (0,2)(0,2) differentials in KP integrable case). In Section 6 we develop the technique of computations with the Gaussian integrals and their connection to the ingredients of the x−yx-y swap relations. This section is the technical core of this paper. Finally, in Section 7 we present necessary details to complete the proof of identities of Section 4.

It is important to mention that we assume that the reader is a bit familiar with Kadomtsev–Petviashvili hierarchy, which we call elsewhere KP hierarchy for brevity. Otherwise we refer to [MJD12] as the main source on this topic. Also we do not recall at all the concept of spectral curve topological recursion. As we explain below, in many cases it is sufficient to know that it can be replaced by the x−yx-y swap formula, and otherwise we refer the reader to the foundational survey [EO09] and more recent sources (e.g. [ABDBKS25]) for precise statements that we use.

2. Introduction, part 1: first layer of concepts and results

2.1. nn-point differentials

Let Σ\Sigma be a smooth complex curve that we refer below as the spectral curve. The main object of this paper is a collection of nn-differentials ωn(g)\omega^{(g)}_{n} on Σn\Sigma^{n} defined for all g≥0g\geq 0, n≥1n\geq 1.

We assume that all ωn(g)\omega^{(g)}_{n}’s are symmetric and meromorphic with no poles on the diagonals for (g,n)≠(0,2)(g,n)\neq(0,2), and ω2(0)\omega^{(0)}_{2} is also symmetric and meromorphic but it has a second order pole on the diagonal with biresidue 11. It will be convenient to arrange the nn-differentials ωn(g)\omega^{(g)}_{n}, g≥0g\geq 0, for each fixed nn into generating series:

(2.1) ωn≔∑g=0∞ℏ2​g−2+n​ωn(g).\omega_{n}\coloneqq\sum_{g=0}^{\infty}\hbar^{2g-2+n}\omega^{(g)}_{n}.

Systems of nn-point differentials provide a natural and convenient way to assemble the answers to various problems in many interrelated areas of mathematics and theoretical physics, for instance, in matrix models, enumerative algebraic geometry, and combinatorics.

2.2. KP integrability

KP integrability plays a prominent role in mathematics and mathematical physics, the basic reference is [MJD12].

The KP hierarchy can be seen as an integrable system of PDEs for a so-called tau function that can be written in several different ways. For this paper it is important that for formal solutions it has an interpretation as Plücker relations for the open part of semi-infinite Grassmannian. These relations ensure that a particular vector v∈⨁λvλv\in\bigoplus_{\lambda}v_{\lambda} (here vλ=zλ1−1∧zλ2−2∧zλ3−3∧…v_{\lambda}=z^{\lambda_{1}-1}\wedge z^{\lambda_{2}-2}\wedge z^{\lambda_{3}-3}\wedge\dots and the sum is taken over all partitions λ⊢d\lambda\vdash d, d∈ℤ≥0d\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} arranged as λ1≥λ2≥λ3≥…\lambda_{1}\geq\lambda_{2}\geq\lambda_{3}\geq...) can be represented as

(2.2) v=Φ1∧Φ2∧Φ3∧…,\displaystyle v=\Phi_{1}\wedge\Phi_{2}\wedge\Phi_{3}\wedge\dots,

where Φi=z−i​(1+O⁡(z))\Phi_{i}=z^{-i}(1+O(z)). For a vector vv, the corresponding tau function τv\tau_{v} can be written in formal variables p1,p2,…p_{1},p_{2},\dots as

(2.3) τv≔⟨0|​exp⁡(∑i=1∞pii​Ji)​v.\displaystyle\tau_{v}\coloneqq\langle 0|\exp\left({\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}}\frac{p_{i}}{i}J_{i}\right)v.

Here Ja=∑i∈ℤ:ψi−aψ∗i:J_{a}=\sum_{i\in\mathbb{Z}}:\psi_{i-a}\psi^{*}_{i}:, where ψi=zi∧\psi_{i}=z^{i}\wedge, ψ∗i=∂zi\psi^{*}_{i}=\partial_{z^{i}}, the normal ordering is defined as :ψi​ψj∗:=ψi​ψj∗:\psi_{i}\psi^{*}_{j}:=\psi_{i}\psi^{*}_{j} for j≥0j\geq 0 and −ψj∗​ψi-\psi^{*}_{j}\psi_{i} for j<0j<0, and ⟨0|\langle 0| is the operator which gives a constant term of the formal power series in variables p1,p2,….p_{1},p_{2},\ldots. The condition given by Equation (2.2) is then equivalent to the Hirota bilinear identity

(2.4) ∮∞e∑i=1∞pi−qii​zie∑i=1∞z−i(∂qi−∂pi)τv(p1,p2,…)τv(q1,q2,…)dz=0.\displaystyle\oint_{\infty}e^{\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{p_{i}-q_{i}}{i}z^{i}}e^{\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}z^{-i}(\partial_{q_{i}}-\partial_{p_{i}})}\tau_{v}(p_{1},p_{2},\dots)\tau_{v}(q_{1},q_{2},\dots)dz=0.

There is a version of it that takes into account topological expansions of the corresponding τ\tau functions, which is sometimes called the ℏ\hbar-KP integrability, see [TT95].

2.3. KP integrability as a property of a system of differentials

To pass from a system of differentials to KP tau functions, we need the following definition:

Definition 2.1.

A point o∈Σo\in\Sigma is called regular for the system of differentials {ωn(g)}\{\omega^{(g)}_{n}\} if ωn(g)−δ(g,n),(0,2)​d​x1​d​x2(x1−x2)2\omega^{(g)}_{n}-\delta_{(g,n),(0,2)}\frac{dx_{1}dx_{2}}{(x_{1}-x_{2})^{2}} is regular at (o,…,o)∈Σn(o,\dots,o)\in\Sigma^{n} for all (g,n)∈ℤ≥0×ℤ>0(g,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\times\mathbb{Z}_{>0}, (g,n)≠(0,1)(g,n)\not=(0,1), where xx is a local coordinate on Σ\Sigma at oo.

Remark 2.2.

Note that the regularity condition for {ωn(g)}\{\omega^{(g)}_{n}\} is independent of a choice of local coordinate. Note also that we have no condition for ω1(0)\omega^{(0)}_{1}.

For a regular point oo, and an arbitrary local coordinate xx, the forms ωn(g)\omega^{(g)}_{n} can be expanded into a series

(2.5) ωn=∑g=0∞ℏ2​g−2+n​ωn(g)=δn,2​d​x1​d​x2(x1−x2)2+∑k1,…,kn=1∞fk1,…,kn​∏i=1nki​xiki−1​d​xi,\omega_{n}=\sum_{g=0}^{\infty}\hbar^{2g-2+n}\omega^{(g)}_{n}=\delta_{n,2}\tfrac{dx_{1}dx_{2}}{(x_{1}-x_{2})^{2}}+\sum_{k_{1},\dots,k_{n}=1}^{\infty}f_{k_{1},\dots,k_{n}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}k_{i}x_{i}^{k_{i}-1}dx_{i},

where the coefficients fk1,…,knf_{k_{1},\dots,k_{n}} expand as ∑g=0∞ℏ2​g−2+n​fk1,…,kn(g)\sum_{g=0}^{\infty}\hbar^{2g-2+n}f^{(g)}_{k_{1},\dots,k_{n}}. Introduce the associated potential F=Fo,xF=F_{o,x} as

(2.6) F⁡(p1,p2,…)≔∑g,nℏ2​g−2+n​Fn(g)=∑n=1∞1n!​∑k1,…,kn=1∞fk1,…,kn​pk1​…​pkn,F(p_{1},p_{2},\dots)\coloneqq\sum_{g,n}\hbar^{2g-2+n}F^{(g)}_{n}=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{k_{1},\dots,k_{n}=1}^{\infty}f_{k_{1},\dots,k_{n}}p_{k_{1}}\dots p_{k_{n}},

where Fn(g)F^{(g)}_{n} are homogeneous formal series of degree nn.

This way we associate to a given collection of differentials ωn(g)\omega^{(g)}_{n} a large family of potentials Fo,xF_{o,x}: the freedom in its definition consists of the choice of a regular point oo and the choice of a local coordinate xx at oo. We would like to study conditions assuring that

(2.7) Zo,x≔exp⁡(Fo,x)Z_{o,x}\coloneqq\exp(F_{o,x})

is a tau function of the KP hierarchy.

Theorem 2.3.

The KP integrability is an internal property of the collection of differentials: if Zo,xZ_{o,x} is a tau function of KP hierarchy for some choice of a regular point oo and a coordinate xx at this point, then it is a tau function of KP hierarchy for any other choice of a regular point and a local coordinate at that point.

We prove this theorem in Section 3.2.

Remark 2.4.

The choice of ω1(0)\omega^{(0)}_{1} does not affect the KP integrability property, it can be chosen in an arbitrary way. For definiteness, in (2.5) and in all expressions below which contain a summation over genus we do not include the terms with (g,n)=(0,1)(g,n)=(0,1).

Remark 2.5.

A change of the local spectral parameter (local coordinate on the spectral curve) is known to provide a symmetry of the KP hierarchy [Shi86], given by an element of the Virasoro subgroup of G​L^∞\widehat{GL}_{\infty}.

2.4. x−yx-y swap relation

The x−yx-y swap relation is given by several equivalent formulas that act on a system of differentials ωn(g)\omega^{(g)}_{n} and produce a new system of differentials denoted by ωn∨,(g)\omega^{\vee,(g)}_{n}. In order to apply it we need to assume that Σ\Sigma is endowed a pair of meromorphic functions on it, denoted by xx and yy. We present the x−yx-y swap relation here in the form given in [Hoc23, ABDBKS25].

As we have mentioned in Remark 2.4, the choice of ω1(0)\omega^{(0)}_{1} is irrelevant for the KP integrability property, so for instance we can fix it to be ω1(0)=−y​d​x\omega^{(0)}_{1}=-ydx following the tradition coming from the theory of spectral curve topological recursion. However, it will be more convenient to fix it as ω1(0)=0\omega^{(0)}_{1}=0 and to single out the contribution of −y​d​x-ydx in the formulas explicitly.

Then we define a new system of differentials ωn∨,(g)\omega^{\vee,(g)}_{n} given by

(2.8) ωn∨,(g)​(z⟦n⟧)∏i=1nd​yi=(−1)n​[ℏ2​g]⁡∏i=1n∑ri=0∞∂yiri[uiri]​d​xid​yi​e−ui(𝒮(uiℏ∂xi)−1)yiui∑Γℏ2​g​(Γ)|Aut⁡(Γ)|∏e∈E⁡(Γ)∏j=1|e|⌊(u~j,x~j)→(ue⁡(j),xe⁡(j))u~j𝒮(ℏu~j∂x~j)∑g~=0∞ℏ2​g~ω~|e|(g~)​(z~⟦|e|⟧)∏j=1|e|d​x~j.\frac{\omega_{n}^{\vee,(g)}(z_{\llbracket n\rrbracket})}{\prod_{i=1}^{n}dy_{i}}=(-1)^{n}\mathop{[{\hbar}^{2g}]}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{r_{i}=0}^{\infty}\partial_{y_{i}}^{r_{i}}[u_{i}^{r_{i}}]\frac{dx_{i}}{dy_{i}}\frac{e^{-u_{i}(\mathcal{S}(u_{i}\hbar\partial_{x_{i}})-1)y_{i}}}{u_{i}}\\ \sum_{\Gamma}\frac{\hbar^{2g(\Gamma)}}{|\mathrm{Aut}(\Gamma)|}\prod_{e\in E(\Gamma)}\prod_{j=1}^{|e|}\mathop{\big\lfloor_{{(\tilde{u}_{j},\tilde{x}_{j})}\to{(u_{e(j)},x_{e(j)})}}}\tilde{u}_{j}\mathcal{S}(\hbar\tilde{u}_{j}\partial_{\tilde{x}_{j}})\sum_{\tilde{g}=0}^{\infty}\hbar^{2\tilde{g}}\frac{\tilde{\omega}^{(\tilde{g})}_{|e|}(\tilde{z}_{\llbracket|e|\rrbracket})}{\prod_{j=1}^{|e|}d\tilde{x}_{j}}.

Here xi=x⁡(zi)x_{i}=x(z_{i}), yi=y⁡(zi)y_{i}=y(z_{i}), where ziz_{i} is a point on the ii-th copy of Σ\Sigma in Σn\Sigma^{n}; the same applies to x~i=x⁡(z~i)\tilde{x}_{i}=x(\tilde{z}_{i}). The sum is taken over all connected bipartite graphs (or hypergraphs or just graphs with multiedges, for brevity) Γ\Gamma with nn labeled vertices and multiedges of arbitrary index ≥1\geq 1, where the index of a multiedge is the number of its “legs” and we denote it by |e||e|. For a multiedge ee with index |e||e| we control its attachment to the vertices by the associated map e:⟦|e|⟧→⟦n⟧e\colon\llbracket|e|\rrbracket\to\llbracket n\rrbracket that we denote also by ee, abusing notation (so e⁡(j)e(j) is the label of the vertex to which the jj-th “leg” of the multiedge ee is attached). Terms with (g,n)=(0,1)(g,n)=(0,1) are excluded from the summation, and ω~2(0)​(x~1,x~2)=ω2(0)​(x~1,x~2)−d​x~1​d​x~2(x~1−x~2)2\tilde{\omega}^{(0)}_{2}(\tilde{x}_{1},\tilde{x}_{2})=\omega^{(0)}_{2}(\tilde{x}_{1},\tilde{x}_{2})-\frac{d\tilde{x}_{1}d\tilde{x}_{2}}{(\tilde{x}_{1}-\tilde{x}_{2})^{2}} if e⁡(1)=e⁡(2)e(1)=e(2), and ω~2(0)​(x~1,x~2)=ω2(0)​(x~1,x~2)\tilde{\omega}^{(0)}_{2}(\tilde{x}_{1},\tilde{x}_{2})=\omega^{(0)}_{2}(\tilde{x}_{1},\tilde{x}_{2}) otherwise. For all (g,n)≠(0,2)(g,n)\not=(0,2) we simply have ω~n(g)=ωn(g)\tilde{\omega}^{(g)}_{n}=\omega^{(g)}_{n}. By g⁡(Γ)g(\Gamma) we denote the first Betti number of Γ\Gamma. By [ℏ2​g][\hbar^{2g}] (respectively, [wiki][w_{i}^{k_{i}}]) we denote the operator that extracts the corresponding coefficient from the whole expression to the right of it. By ⌊a→b\mathop{\big\lfloor_{{a}\to{b}}} we denote the operator of substitution a→ba\to b. The function 𝒮⁡(z)\mathcal{S}(z) is defined as

(2.9) 𝒮⁡(z)≔ez/2−e−z/2z.\displaystyle\mathcal{S}(z)\coloneqq\frac{e^{z/2}-e^{-z/2}}{z}.

In the theory of topological recursion, this formula expresses the swap of xx and yy [ABDBKS25], see also [Hoc24] in genus 00. It also expresses a higher genera extension of the correspondence between moments and cumulants in the higher order free probability theory [BCGFLS21].

Remark 2.6.

Note that it is absolutely non-trivial that the right hand side of (2.8) does not have poles on the diagonals. It follows from [ABDBKS25, Proposition 4.6] where we proved it using formal expansion in the Fock space.

Remark 2.7.

The formulation of the x−yx-y swap relation does not explicitly require that xx and yy are meromorphic; it is sufficient to assume that d​xdx and d​ydy are meromorphic (so these 11-forms might have non-trivial residues). It is possible to extend the results of this paper that concern KP integrability to this more general setup, see [ABDBKS24].

2.5. x−yx-y swap relation and KP integrability

One of the main results of this paper can be formulated as follows:

Theorem 2.8.

The x−yx-y swap relation preserves KP integrability: the original system of differentials ωn(g)\omega^{(g)}_{n} is KP integrable (in the sense of Theorem 2.3) if and only if the dual system of differentials ωn∨,(g)\omega^{\vee,(g)}_{n} is KP integrable.

This theorem is proved in Section 4.3.

On the one hand, this theorem is quite natural since the x−yx-y swap relation is itself coming from an element of G​L^∞\widehat{GL}_{\infty} that preserves KP integrability of tau functions. Namely, if there exists a point o∈Σo\in\Sigma regular for the differentials {ωn(g)}\{\omega_{n}^{(g)}\} such that functions xx and yy have at this point a simple zero and a simple pole, respectively, and x⁡(z)​y​(z)→1x(z)y(z)\to 1 as z→oz\to o, then (see [ABDBKS25]) we have

(2.10) Zo,y−1∨=𝒟1+θ​Zo,x,\displaystyle Z^{\vee}_{o,y^{-1}}=\mathcal{D}_{1+\theta}Z_{o,x},

where the operator 𝒟1+θ\mathcal{D}_{1+\theta} defined as a diagonal operator in the basis of Schur polynomials sλ≔τvλs_{\lambda}\coloneqq\tau_{v_{\lambda}} acting as

(2.11) 𝒟1+θ:sλ↦(∏(i,j)∈λ(1+ℏ​(i−j)))​sλ\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{1+\theta}\colon s_{\lambda}\mapsto\Big(\prod_{(i,j)\in\lambda}(1+\hbar(i-j))\Big)s_{\lambda}

is known to preserve the KP integrability. On the other hand, in the absence of a regular point with these properties, Theorem 2.8 becomes a very deep statement on the structure of x−yx-y swap relation that requires a full revision of our understanding of the meaning and interpretations of the latter formula. We prove it at the end of Section 4.3.

2.6. Higher BGW tau functions

Topological recursion associates to a particular input that consists of a spectral curve Σ\Sigma, functions xx and yy on Σ\Sigma, and a choice of the Bergman kernel, the output that consists of a system of symmetric nn-differentials ωn(g)\omega^{(g)}_{n} on Σn\Sigma^{n}. We refer to [EO09] and [BE13] for the necessary definitions but omit them in this paper for the following reason. In the context of this paper in the special case when Σ=ℂ​P1\Sigma=\mathbb{C}P^{1} and yy is an affine coordinate, the resulting differentials ωn(g)\omega^{(g)}_{n} are obtained by the y−xy-x swap relation (that is, the inverse of x−yx-y swap relation, which is given by (2.8) with the interchanged xx and yy and ωn(g)\omega^{(g)}_{n}’s and ωn∨,(g)\omega^{\vee,(g)}_{n}’s, respectively) applied to {ωn(g),∨}g≥0,n≥1\{\omega^{(g),\vee}_{n}\}_{g\geq 0,n\geq 1} defined as ω1(0),∨=−x​d​y\omega^{(0),\vee}_{1}=-xdy, OPENω2(0),∨=d​y1​d​y2/(y1−y2))2\omega^{(0),\vee}_{2}=dy_{1}dy_{2}/(y_{1}-y_{2}))^{2}, and ωn(g),∨=0\omega^{(g),\vee}_{n}=0 for 2​g−2+n>02g-2+n>0, see [ABDBKS25, Section 7]. This description is sufficient to formulate the following result.

Consider a system of differentials constructed with the input given by Σ=ℂ​P1\Sigma=\mathbb{C}P^{1} with a global rational coordinate zz, x=zr/rx=z^{r}/r, and y=z−1y=z^{-1}, and B=d​z1​d​z2(z1−z2)2B=\frac{dz_{1}dz_{2}}{(z_{1}-z_{2})^{2}}. One can show that z=∞z=\infty is a regular point for this system of differentials, so we consider the partition function Z∞,z−1Z_{\infty,z^{-1}}.

Theorem 2.9.

The partition function Z∞,z−1Z_{\infty,z^{-1}} is given by the following matrix integral:

(2.12) Z∞,z−1=∫ℋNd​M​exp⁡(1ℏ​Tr⁡(Λr​Mr+M1−rr⁡(r−1)−ℏ​N​ln⁡M))∫ℋNd​M​exp⁡(1ℏ​Tr⁡(M1−rr⁡(r−1)−ℏ​N​ln⁡M)),\displaystyle Z_{\infty,z^{-1}}=\frac{\int_{\mathcal{H}_{N}}dM\exp\bigg(\frac{1}{{\hbar}}\Tr\Big(\frac{\Lambda^{r}M}{r}+\frac{M^{1-r}}{r(r-1)}-{\hbar}N\ln M\Big)\bigg)}{\int_{\mathcal{H}_{N}}dM\exp\bigg(\frac{1}{{\hbar}}\Tr\Big(\frac{M^{1-r}}{r(r-1)}-{\hbar}N\ln M\Big)\bigg)},

where ℋN\mathcal{H}_{N} is the space N×NN\times N Hermitian matrices and d​MdM is the standard measure on it, and the variables pip_{i} are the Miwa variables, pi=Tr⁡Λ−ip_{i}=\Tr\Lambda^{-i}, i=1,2,…i=1,2,\dots.

This theorem is proven in Section 3.7.

Remark 2.10.

The latter matrix integral is considered as formal matrix integral, asymptotically expanded in the vicinity of Gaussian point, c.f. [MMS96, AD25] and Section 6.1.

Remark 2.11.

The latter matrix integral is considered in [MMS96, AD25] and is known as a higher Brézin–Gross–Witten tau function, or simply rr-BGW tau function. The statement of Theorem 2.9 was conjectured in [AD25, Conjecture 4.1] and [CGFG23, Conjecture F].

Remark 2.12.

Partition function Z∞,z−1Z_{\infty,z^{-1}} has a geometric meaning. The formal power series expansion of its logarithm gives the intersection numbers of the tautological ψ\psi-classes with the so-called rr-theta classes Θg,nr\Theta^{r}_{g,n} on the moduli spaces of curves ℳ¯g,n\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n} [CGFG23]. In particular, for r=2r=2 it is reduced to a generating series of ψ\psi- and a combination of κ\kappa-classes with some distinguished polynomial behavior [KN24].

Remark 2.13.

From the identification with the matrix integral it immediately follows [MMS96] that Z∞,z−1Z_{\infty,z^{-1}} is a tau function of the rr-reduction of the KP hierarchy (or Gelfand–Dickey hierarchy).

3. Introduction, part 2: a deeper look into KP integrability and x−yx-y swap relation

3.1. Baker–Akhiezer kernel and determinantal formulas

For a given formal power series τ=τ⁡(p1,p2,…)=1+O⁡(p1,p2,…)\tau=\tau(p_{1},p_{2},\dots)=1+O(p_{1},p_{2},\dots) the kernel K⁡(x1,x2)K(x_{1},x_{2}) is defined as

(3.1) K(x1,x2)≔1x1−x2(∏i=1∞⌊pi→x1i−x2i)τ.\displaystyle K(x_{1},x_{2})\coloneqq\frac{1}{x_{1}-x_{2}}\Big(\prod_{i=1}^{\infty}\mathop{\big\lfloor_{{p_{i}}\to{x_{1}^{i}-x_{2}^{i}}}}\Big)\tau.

If τ\tau is a tau function of the KP hierarchy, then KK is called the Baker–Akhiezer kernel. It is a sum of one specific term (x1−x2)−1(x_{1}-x_{2})^{-1} and some formal power series in x1,x2x_{1},x_{2}.

Under the assumption of KP integrability it characterizes the solution uniquely, using formuals (3.3) and (3.1), and can be used to express the formal nn-point functions WnW_{n} associated to τ\tau by the following formulas. Let

(3.2) Wn(x1,…,xn)≔⌊p1,p2,…→0(∏i=1n∑k=1∞kxik−1∂pk)logτ,\displaystyle W_{n}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\coloneqq\mathop{\big\lfloor_{{p_{1},p_{2},\dots}\to{0}}}\Big(\prod_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}kx_{i}^{k-1}\partial_{p_{k}}\Big)\log\tau,

then we have:

(3.3) W1​(x1)\displaystyle W_{1}(x_{1}) =limx1′→x1(K⁡(x1,x1′)−1x1−x1′);\displaystyle=\lim_{x_{1}^{\prime}\to x_{1}}\Big(K(x_{1},x_{1}^{\prime})-\frac{1}{x_{1}-x_{1}^{\prime}}\Big);
W2​(x1,x2)\displaystyle W_{2}(x_{1},x_{2}) =−K⁡(x1,x2)​K​(x2,x1)−1(x1−x2)2;\displaystyle=-K(x_{1},x_{2})K(x_{2},x_{1})-\frac{1}{(x_{1}-x_{2})^{2}};
Wn​(x⟦n⟧)\displaystyle W_{n}(x_{\llbracket n\rrbracket}) =(−1)n−1​∑σ∈Cn∏i=1nK⁡(xi,xσ⁡(i)),\displaystyle=(-1)^{n-1}\sum_{\sigma\in C_{n}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}K(x_{i},x_{\sigma(i)}), n≥3,\displaystyle n\geq 3,

where Cn⊂SnC_{n}\subset S_{n} is the set of cycles of length nn. These formulas are called the determinantal formulas and are direct consequences of the Wick formula [Zho15]. More precisely, from [Zho15, Section 5] we have:

Lemma 3.1.

A formal power series τ\tau is a KP tau function if and only if Equations (3.3) hold.

3.2. Determinantal formulas for systems of differentials and a proof of Theorem 2.3

In the context of KP integrability as a property of a system of differentials, we consider a given system of differentials {ωn(g)}\{\omega^{(g)}_{n}\}, and we assume that the tau function and the corresponding kernel KK of the previous section are associated with a particular choice of the regular point oo of the spectral curve and the local coordinate xx at this point. Since linear terms of the potential do not affect KP integrability, let us assume for definiteness that

(3.4) ω1(0)≔0,\omega^{(0)}_{1}\coloneqq 0,

see Remark 2.4.

We introduce an invariant version of the Baker–Akhiezer kernel as the bi-half-differential

(3.5) 𝕂⁡(x1,x2)≔K⁡(x1,x2)​d​x1​d​x2.\mathbb{K}(x_{1},x_{2})\coloneqq K(x_{1},x_{2})\sqrt{dx_{1}dx_{2}}.
Remark 3.2.

By a half-differential we understand a local section of a line bundle LL on Σ\Sigma such that L⊗2≅KΣL^{\otimes 2}\cong K_{\Sigma}. A particular choice of LL (known as theta characteristic) is fixed and is the same for all variables, and the exposition below doesn’t depend on this choice.

Note that if τ=Zo,x\tau=Z_{o,x} via (2.5)–(2.7) for the system of differentials {ωn(g)}\{\omega^{(g)}_{n}\}, then the nn-point functions WnW_{n} defined in (3.2) can be expressed in terms of the {ωn(g)}\{\omega^{(g)}_{n}\}’s themselves as follows:

(3.6) Wn=ωn∏i=1nd​xi−δn,2​1(x1−x2)2,\displaystyle W_{n}=\frac{\omega_{n}}{\prod_{i=1}^{n}dx_{i}}-\delta_{n,2}\frac{1}{(x_{1}-x_{2})^{2}},

where ωn=∑g=0∞ℏ2​g−2+n​ωn(g)\omega_{n}=\sum_{g=0}^{\infty}\hbar^{2g-2+n}\omega^{(g)}_{n}.

Then the determinantal formulas (3.3) in the KP integrable case can be rewritten as

(3.7) ω1​(x1)\displaystyle\omega_{1}(x_{1}) =limx1′→x1(𝕂⁡(x1,x1′)−d​x1​d​x1′x1−x1′);\displaystyle=\lim_{x_{1}^{\prime}\to x_{1}}\Big(\mathbb{K}(x_{1},x_{1}^{\prime})-\frac{\sqrt{dx_{1}dx^{\prime}_{1}}}{x_{1}-x_{1}^{\prime}}\Big);
ωn​(x⟦n⟧)\displaystyle\omega_{n}(x_{\llbracket n\rrbracket}) =(−1)n−1​∑σ∈Cn∏i=1n𝕂⁡(xi,xσ⁡(i)),\displaystyle=(-1)^{n-1}\sum_{\sigma\in C_{n}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{K}(x_{i},x_{\sigma(i)}), n≥2.\displaystyle n\geq 2.

Note that we consider (3.5)–(3.7) at the moment as equalities of power expansions at the point oo in the local coordinate xx of the spectral curve.

Remark 3.3.

Equation (3.7) is not a completely straightforward rewriting of (3.3); the identification of the formulas for ω1\omega_{1} and W1W_{1} uses a corollary of the KP integrability equations for ω2(0)\omega^{(0)}_{2} under the assumption (3.4), cf. Sections 3.3 and 5 below.

Proposition 3.4.

The kernel 𝕂\mathbb{K} extends as a formal series in ℏ\hbar whose coefficients are global meromorphic differentials on Σ2\Sigma^{2} defined in a vicinity of the diagonal. The introduced differential 𝕂\mathbb{K} is independent of a choice of the point oo and of the local coordinate xx, and is uniquely determined by the system of differentials {ωn(g)}\{\omega^{(g)}_{n}\}.

Proof.

For the proof we provide an alternative invariant expression for 𝕂\mathbb{K} directly in terms the differentials ωn(g)\omega^{(g)}_{n}:

(3.8) 𝕂⁡(z1,z2)\displaystyle\mathbb{K}(z_{1},z_{2}) ≔d​x1​d​x2x1−x2​exp⁡(∑2​g−2+n>0ℏ2​g−2+nn!​∫z2z1…​∫z2z1ωn(g)+12​∫z2z1∫z2z1(ω2(0)−ω2(0),sing)),\displaystyle\coloneqq\frac{\sqrt{dx_{1}\;dx_{2}}}{x_{1}-x_{2}}\exp\bigg(\sum\limits_{2g-2+n>0}\frac{\hbar^{2g-2+n}}{n!}\int\limits_{z_{2}}^{z_{1}}\dots\int\limits_{z_{2}}^{z_{1}}\omega^{(g)}_{n}+\frac{1}{2}\int\limits_{z_{2}}^{z_{1}}\!\!\int\limits_{z_{2}}^{z_{1}}(\omega^{(0)}_{2}-\omega^{(0),{\rm sing}}_{2})\bigg),
(3.9) ω2(0),sing\displaystyle\omega^{(0),{\rm sing}}_{2} ≔d​x1​d​x2(x1−x2)2.\displaystyle\coloneqq\frac{dx_{1}dx_{2}}{(x_{1}-x_{2})^{2}}.

The integrals ∫z2z1\int_{z_{2}}^{z_{1}} under the exponent in this expression of 𝕂\mathbb{K} are single-valued functions in the vicinity of the diagonal, since we the integral path is chosen in the vicinity of the diagonal. To this end we note that the only possible multi-valuedness can occur in the neighborhood of a simple pole pp of ωn(g)\omega^{(g)}_{n}. In this case we choose a branch of the logarithm of log⁡z1/z2\log{z_{1}/z_{2}} that is a single valued function near (p,p)∈Σ2(p,p)\in\Sigma^{2} once we remove a cut connecting the germs of the divisors z1=pz_{1}=p and z2=pz_{2}=p near the diagonal. We regard 𝕂\mathbb{K} as a (bi-half-)differential on Σ2\Sigma^{2} and use z1z_{1} and z2z_{2} as a notation for the corresponding points of the spectral curve, and xi=x⁡(zi)x_{i}=x(z_{i}). This formula makes sense if z1z_{1} and z2z_{2} are close to one another and is actually a reformulation of (3.1).

The definition (3.8) involves a regularizing term ω2(0),sing\omega^{(0)\rm,sing}_{2} that does depend on a choice of local coordinate xx — the equation does not make sense without this regularizing term. However, it can be easily checked by direct substitution that a change of local coordinate implying the corresponding change of the regularizing term leads to an equivalent equation. Indeed, for any other local coordinate yy near oo, y=y⁡(x)y=y(x), we have:

(3.10) d​y​(x1)​d​y​(x2)(y⁡(x1)−y⁡(x2))2=d​x1​d​x2(x1−x2)2​exp⁡(∫x2x1∫x2x1(d​y​(x1)​d​y​(x2)(y⁡(x1)−y​(x2)2CLOSE−d​x1​d​x2(x1−x2)2)).\frac{dy(x_{1})dy(x_{2})}{(y(x_{1})-y(x_{2}))^{2}}=\frac{dx_{1}dx_{2}}{(x_{1}-x_{2})^{2}}\,\exp\left({\int\limits_{x_{2}}^{x_{1}}\int\limits_{x_{2}}^{x_{1}}\left(\frac{dy(x_{1})dy(x_{2})}{(y(x_{1})-y(x_{2})^{2}}-\frac{dx_{1}dx_{2}}{(x_{1}-x_{2})^{2}}\right)}\right).

If we take for xx any global meromorphic function then the form 𝕂\mathbb{K} defined by (3.8) is also meromorphic in a vicinity of the diagonal in Σ2\Sigma^{2}. This completes the proof. ∎

For the KP integrable cases below this globally defined differential 𝕂\mathbb{K} we also call the Baker–Akhiezer kernel.

Remark 3.5.

By construction, the differential 𝕂\mathbb{K} is singular on the diagonal. However, the difference 𝕂−d​x1​d​x2x1−x2\mathbb{K}-\frac{\sqrt{dx_{1}dx_{2}}}{x_{1}-x_{2}} is regular at x1=x2x_{1}=x_{2} for any choice of the local coordinate xx.

Proof of Theorem 2.3.

Theorem 2.3 is a direct corollary of Proposition 3.4. Indeed, given a system of differentials {ωn(g)}\{\omega^{(g)}_{n}\}, assume that Zo,xZ_{o,x} for a particular regular point oo of the spectral curve and a local coordinate xx is a tau function of the KP hierarchy. Then Equations (3.3), and hence, Equations (3.7) hold in the power expansions at the point (o,…,o)∈Σn(o,\dots,o)\in\Sigma^{n}. But both sides of (3.7) have global invariant meaning, and hence, (3.7) holds true as an equality of global differentials defined in a neighborhood of the diagonal in Σn\Sigma^{n}. It follows that (3.7), and hence, (3.3) hold for the power expansions at any other point regular for all differentials ωn(g)\omega^{(g)}_{n} implying KP integrability of the corresponding potential. ∎

3.3. KP integrability in the semi-classical limit and application to topological recursion

Consider a system of differentials {ωn(g)}\{\omega^{(g)}_{n}\} and assume that they satisfy the KP integrability property in the sense of Theorem 2.3. As we pointed out in Remark 2.4, the (0,1)(0,1) term is irrelevant for the KP integrability property. But then KP integrability implies severe restrictions for the (0,2)(0,2) term (which we call the semi-classical limit) that we formulate now.

Proposition 3.6.

Let {ωn(g)}\{\omega^{(g)}_{n}\} be a system of symmetric meromorphic differentials satisfying KP integrability property in the sense of Theorem 2.3. Let oo be a regular point for this system. Then there exists a local coordinate zz at this point such that the (0,2)(0,2)-term of the corresponding potential Fo,z=log⁡(Zo,z)F_{o,z}=\log(Z_{o,z}) vanishes. Respectively, for this choice of the local coordinate we have

(3.11) ω2(0)=d​z1​d​z2(z1−z2)2.\omega^{(0)}_{2}=\frac{dz_{1}dz_{2}}{(z_{1}-z_{2})^{2}}.

Moreover, such local coordinate zz extends as a global meromorphic function on Σ\Sigma and the above equality holds globally. The function zz with this property is defined uniquely up to a linear fractional transformation.

For the proof of this Proposition see Section 5. Its local version is well known and proved, in particular, in [TT95, Proposition B.2]. This lemma gives a restriction on the global behaviour of ω2(0)\omega^{(0)}_{2} which does not involve any choice of the point and the local coordinate. In particular, observe that the equation z1=z2z_{1}=z_{2} may be satisfied for two distinct points and the divisor of poles of ω2(0)\omega^{(0)}_{2} may have components distinct from the diagonal. The only case when these additional poles do not appear is when zz is of degree 11, that is, when Σ=ℂ​P1\Sigma=\mathbb{C}P^{1} and zz is an affine coordinate. Thus, we have the following immediate corollary:

Corollary 3.7.

If ω2(0)\omega^{(0)}_{2} has no other poles than on the diagonal and {ωn(g)}\{\omega^{(g)}_{n}\} satisfy the KP integrability property, then the spectral curve is rational.

This condition on ω2(0)\omega^{(0)}_{2} is always satisfied, by definition, in the set-up of standard (c.f. [EO09]) topological recursion:

Theorem 3.8.

If the differentials {ωn(g)}\{\omega^{(g)}_{n}\} produced by standard topological recursion are KP integrable, then the spectral curve Σ\Sigma is rational. Moreover, in this case the kernel 𝕂\mathbb{K} is defined globally on Σ2\Sigma^{2} and the determinantal formulas written in Equation (3.7) hold globally on Σn\Sigma^{n}.

Proof.

The second statement follows from the fact that the topological recursion differentials have no residues so that the integrals entering the definition of 𝕂\mathbb{K} under the exponent are univalued in this case. ∎

3.4. x−yx-y swap for Baker–Akhiezer kernel

If the systems of differentials {ωn(g)}\{\omega^{(g)}_{n}\} and hence {ωn∨,(g)}\{\omega^{\vee,(g)}_{n}\} are KP integrable, in the complicated combinatorial expression (2.8) of x−yx-y duality they both can be replaced by a simpler determinantal formulas (3.7). This observation raises a natural question: what happens with the Baker–Akhiezer kernel under the x−yx-y swap? It proves out that there are explicit formulas relating x−yx-y dual kernels.

Let us consider two integral transforms which are inverse to each other.

Proposition 3.9.

Let for some function f∨​(z)f^{\vee}(z)

(3.12) f⁡(z)=i2​π​ℏ​∫f∨​(χ)​y′​(χ)​e1ℏ​(x⁡(z)​(y⁡(z)−y⁡(χ))+∫zχx​𝑑y)​𝑑χ.f(z)=\tfrac{\mathrm{i}}{\sqrt{2\pi\,\hbar}}\int f^{\vee}(\chi)\;y^{\prime}(\chi)\;e^{\frac{1}{\hbar}\left(x(z)(y(z)-y(\chi))+\int_{z}^{\chi}x\,dy\right)}\,d\chi.

Then

(3.13) f∨​(z)=12​π​ℏ​∫f⁡(χ)​x′​(χ)​e−1ℏ​(y⁡(z)​(x⁡(z)−x⁡(χ))+∫zχy​𝑑x)​𝑑χ.f^{\vee}(z)=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\,\hbar}}\int f(\chi)\;x^{\prime}(\chi)\;e^{-\frac{1}{\hbar}\left(y(z)(x(z)-x(\chi))+\int_{z}^{\chi}y\,dx\right)}\,d\chi.

A proof of Proposition 3.9 is given in Section 6.1.

Remark 3.10.

All integrals of this type are understood purely formally in the sense of asymptotic expansions for small absolute value of ℏ\hbar near the critical points χ=z\chi=z. With this convention the expressions become formal Gaussian integrals and the coefficient of each power of ℏ\hbar of this integral is a finite order differential operator applied to f∨f^{\vee} or ff, respectively. We refer to Section 6 for the precise definition and examples of how one can manipulate with these integrals within the framework given by this formal meaning.

Remark 3.11.

We treat the functions in (3.12),(3.13) as symbolic expressions, c.f. (6.8).

Remark 3.12.

Integral transformations considered in this section are inspired by and closely related to the Kontsevich matrix model and its generalizations [Kon92, KMMMZ92, AM92, KM95, MMS96, Ale21]. Relation to matrix models in more detail will be considered elsewhere.

Proposition 3.9 describes an invertible transformation for arbitrary functions x⁡(z)x(z) and y⁡(z)y(z) (there are still some restrictions imposed by Gaussian integrals, see Remark 6.2 below). This type of transformation connects the Baker–Akhiezer kernels on the two sides of the x−yx-y duality.

Theorem 3.13.

The Baker–Akhiezer kernels 𝕂\mathbb{K} and 𝕂∨\mathbb{K}^{\vee} related by the x−yx-y swap are expressed in terms of one another by the following double integrals:

(3.14) K⁡(z1,z2)\displaystyle K(z_{1},z_{2}) =−i2​π​ℏ∬K∨(χ1,χ2)y′(χ1)y′(χ2)dχ1dχ2×\displaystyle=\tfrac{-\mathrm{i}}{2\pi\hbar}\iint K^{\vee}(\chi_{1},\chi_{2})\;y^{\prime}(\chi_{1})y^{\prime}(\chi_{2})\,d\chi_{1}d\chi_{2}\times
e−1ℏ​(x⁡(z2)​(y⁡(z2)−y⁡(χ1))+∫z2χ1x​𝑑y)​e1ℏ​(x⁡(z1)​(y⁡(z1)−y⁡(χ2))+∫z1χ2x​𝑑y);\displaystyle\hskip 85.35826pte^{-\frac{1}{\hbar}\big(x(z_{2})(y(z_{2})-y(\chi_{1}))+\int_{z_{2}}^{\chi_{1}}xdy\big)}e^{\frac{1}{\hbar}\big(x(z_{1})(y(z_{1})-y(\chi_{2}))+\int_{z_{1}}^{\chi_{2}}xdy\big)};
(3.15) K∨​(z1,z2)\displaystyle K^{\vee}(z_{1},z_{2}) =−i2​π​ℏ∬K(χ1,χ2)x′(χ1)x′(χ2)dχ1dχ2×\displaystyle=\tfrac{-\mathrm{i}}{2\pi\hbar}\iint K(\chi_{1},\chi_{2})\;x^{\prime}(\chi_{1})x^{\prime}(\chi_{2})d\chi_{1}d\chi_{2}\times
e−1ℏ​(y⁡(z2)​(x⁡(z2)−x⁡(χ1))+∫z2χ1y​𝑑x)​e1ℏ​(y⁡(z1)​(x⁡(z1)−x⁡(χ2))+∫z1χ2y​𝑑x).\displaystyle\hskip 85.35826pte^{-\frac{1}{\hbar}\big(y(z_{2})(x(z_{2})-x(\chi_{1}))+\int_{z_{2}}^{\chi_{1}}ydx\big)}e^{\frac{1}{\hbar}\big(y(z_{1})(x(z_{1})-x(\chi_{2}))+\int_{z_{1}}^{\chi_{2}}ydx\big)}.

Here 𝕂⁡(z1,z2)=K⁡(z1,z2)​d​x1​d​x2\mathbb{K}(z_{1},z_{2})=K(z_{1},z_{2})\sqrt{dx_{1}dx_{2}}, 𝕂∨​(z1,z2)=K∨​(z1,z2)​d​y1​d​y2\mathbb{K}^{\vee}(z_{1},z_{2})=K^{\vee}(z_{1},z_{2})\sqrt{dy_{1}dy_{2}}, x′=∂zxx^{\prime}=\partial_{z}x, y′=∂zyy^{\prime}=\partial_{z}y.

The contours are assumed to be chosen in such a way that the corresponding symbolic expressions are determined by the order of zeros of (χ1−z2)(\chi_{1}-z_{2}) and (χ2−z1)(\chi_{2}-z_{1}) near the critical point, see details in Section 6. Theorem 3.13 is proved in Section 4.2.

Remark 3.14.

The fact that transformations given by (3.14) and (3.15) are inverse to each other is a direct corollary of Proposition 3.9.

3.5. x−yx-y dual of a trivial case

An important special case of Theorem 3.13 concerns the situation when the x−yx-y dual side is known to be trivial.

We assume that ω0∨,(2)=d​z1​d​z2(z1−z2)2\omega^{\vee,(2)}_{0}=\tfrac{dz_{1}dz_{2}}{(z_{1}-z_{2})^{2}} and for all (g,n)≠(0,2)(g,n)\not=(0,2) ωn∨,(g)=0\omega^{\vee,(g)}_{n}=0. Here zz is a meromorphic function on Σ\Sigma that can serve as a coordinate at the point o∈Σo\in\Sigma. In this case Zo,z∨=1Z^{\vee}_{o,z}=1 and under the x−yx-y duality relation we have the following immediate corollary of Theorem 3.13.

Corollary 3.15.

The Baker–Akhiezer kernel is given by the double integral:

(3.16) 𝕂⁡(z1,z2)d​z1​d​z2\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{K}(z_{1},z_{2})}{\sqrt{dz_{1}dz_{2}}} =−i​x′​(z1)​x′​(z2)2​π​ℏ∬y′​(χ1)​y′​(χ2)χ1−χ2dχ1dχ2×\displaystyle=\tfrac{-\mathrm{i}\sqrt{x^{\prime}(z_{1})x^{\prime}(z_{2})}}{2\pi\hbar}\iint\frac{\sqrt{y^{\prime}(\chi_{1})y^{\prime}(\chi_{2})}}{\chi_{1}-\chi_{2}}\,d\chi_{1}d\chi_{2}\times
e−1ℏ​(x⁡(z2)​(y⁡(z2)−y⁡(χ1))+∫z2χ1x​𝑑y)​e1ℏ​(x⁡(z1)​(y⁡(z1)−y⁡(χ2))+∫z1χ2x​𝑑y).\displaystyle\hskip 85.35826pte^{-\frac{1}{\hbar}\big(x(z_{2})(y(z_{2})-y(\chi_{1}))+\int_{z_{2}}^{\chi_{1}}xdy\big)}e^{\frac{1}{\hbar}\big(x(z_{1})(y(z_{1})-y(\chi_{2}))+\int_{z_{1}}^{\chi_{2}}xdy\big)}.

Note that in the KP integrable case the kernel 𝕂\mathbb{K} carries the complete information on the corresponding KP tau functions. Let (o,z)(o,z) be a regular point for all differentials and a local coordinate at this point, respectively. Then, the semi-infinite plane corresponding to the tau function Z=Zo,zZ=Z_{o,z} is spanned by the Taylor coefficients of the expansion of 𝕂⁡(z1,z2)/d​z1​d​z2\mathbb{K}(z_{1},z_{2})/\sqrt{dz_{1}dz_{2}} in z2z_{2}. More explicitly, the Baker–Akhiezer kernel can be seen as a generating series for a basis in the semi-infinite plane determining ZZ. Namely, choose an arbitrary basis Φ1−j∗​(z)\Phi^{*}_{1-j}(z), j=1,2,…j=1,2,\dots in the space of regular power series in zz and expand 𝕂\mathbb{K} in this basis with respect to z2z_{2},

(3.17) 𝕂⁡(z1,z2)=∑i=1∞Φi​(z1)​Φ1−i∗​(z2)​d​z1​d​z2.\mathbb{K}(z_{1},z_{2})=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\Phi_{i}(z_{1})\Phi^{*}_{1-i}(z_{2})\sqrt{dz_{1}dz_{2}}.

Then the coefficients Φi\Phi_{i} of this expansion generate the corresponding semi-infinite plane as well as the corresponding decomposable vector v=Φ1∧Φ2∧…v=\Phi_{1}\wedge\Phi_{2}\wedge\dots. A different basis Φ1−j∗\Phi^{*}_{1-j} in the space of regular series leads to a different collection of vectors Φi\Phi_{i} but the linear span of these vectors is the same. Conversely, any basis Φi\Phi_{i} in the semi-infinite plane associated with the tau function can be realized by an expansion of the form (3.17). Namely, the corresponding basis Φ1−i∗\Phi^{*}_{1-i} in the space of regular series is orthogonal dual to the basis of functions Φi\Phi_{i} in the following sense

(3.18) resz=0Φi​(z)​Φj∗​(z)​d​z=δi+j,1.\displaystyle\mathop{\rm res}_{z=0}\Phi_{i}(z)\Phi^{*}_{j}(z)dz=\delta_{i+j,1}.

For convenience, we will always assume that the chosen basis in the semi-infinite plane satisfies Φi​(z)=z−i​(1+O⁡(z))\Phi_{i}(z)=z^{-i}(1+O(z)) which is equivalent to the requirement Φ1−i∗​(z)=zi−1​(1+O⁡(z))\Phi^{*}_{1-i}(z)=z^{i-1}(1+O(z)).

Then, in the setting of Corollary 3.15, and under an extra assumption of the local behavior of x′​y′x^{\prime}y^{\prime} at the point oo, we have the following explicit formula for Φi\Phi_{i}, i≥1i\geq 1.

Corollary 3.16.

In the setting of Corollary 3.15, assume x′​y′x^{\prime}y^{\prime} has a pole of degree ≥3\geq 3 at z=0z=0. For the x−yx-y dual system {ωn(g)}\{\omega^{(g)}_{n}\} the corresponding partition function Zo,zZ_{o,z} is a KP tau function corresponding to the semi-infinite plane spanned by

(3.19) Φi​(z)\displaystyle\Phi_{i}(z) =−x′​(z)2​π​ℏ​∫χ−i​y′​(χ)​e1ℏ​(x⁡(z)​(y⁡(z)−y⁡(χ))+∫zχx​𝑑y)​𝑑χ,\displaystyle=\sqrt{\tfrac{-x^{\prime}(z)}{2\pi\hbar}}\int\chi^{-i}\;\sqrt{{y^{\prime}(\chi)}}\;e^{\frac{1}{\hbar}\big(x(z)(y(z)-y(\chi))+\int_{z}^{\chi}xdy\big)}d\chi, i≥1.\displaystyle i\geq 1.
Proof.

Indeed, rewrite an expansion of Equation (3.16) as

(3.20) 𝕂⁡(z1,z2)d​z1​d​z2\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{K}(z_{1},z_{2})}{\sqrt{dz_{1}dz_{2}}} =−x′​(z1)​x′​(z2)2​π​ℏ∬∑i=1∞χ1i−1χ2iy′​(χ1)​y′​(χ2)dχ1dχ2×\displaystyle=\tfrac{\sqrt{-x^{\prime}(z_{1})x^{\prime}(z_{2})}}{2\pi\hbar}\iint\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{\chi_{1}^{i-1}}{\chi_{2}^{i}}{\sqrt{y^{\prime}(\chi_{1})y^{\prime}(\chi_{2})}}\,d\chi_{1}d\chi_{2}\times
e−1ℏ​(x⁡(z2)​(y⁡(z2)−y⁡(χ1))+∫z2χ1x​𝑑y)​e1ℏ​(x⁡(z1)​(y⁡(z1)−y⁡(χ2))+∫z1χ2x​𝑑y)\displaystyle\hskip 85.35826pte^{-\frac{1}{\hbar}\big(x(z_{2})(y(z_{2})-y(\chi_{1}))+\int_{z_{2}}^{\chi_{1}}xdy\big)}e^{\frac{1}{\hbar}\big(x(z_{1})(y(z_{1})-y(\chi_{2}))+\int_{z_{1}}^{\chi_{2}}xdy\big)}
=∑i=1∞Φi​(z1)​Φ1−i∗​(z2),\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\Phi_{i}(z_{1})\Phi^{*}_{1-i}(z_{2}),

where Φi\Phi_{i} is given by (3.19) and

(3.21) Φ1−i∗​(z)=x′​(z)2​π​ℏ​∫χi−1​y′​(χ)​𝑑χ​e−1ℏ​(x⁡(z)​(y⁡(z)−y⁡(χ))+∫zχx​𝑑y).\Phi^{*}_{1-i}(z)=\sqrt{\tfrac{x^{\prime}(z)}{2\pi\hbar}}\int\chi^{i-1}\sqrt{y^{\prime}(\chi)}\,d\chi e^{-\frac{1}{\hbar}\big(x(z)(y(z)-y(\chi))+\int_{z}^{\chi}xdy\big)}.

The condition that x′​y′x^{\prime}y^{\prime} has a pole of degree ≥3\geq 3 at z=0z=0 and the analysis of the corresponding Gaussian integrals imply that the second factor Φ1−i∗​(z2)\Phi^{*}_{1-i}(z_{2}) in the sum is regular in z2z_{2} and has the form z2i−1​(1+O⁡(z2))z_{2}^{i-1}(1+O(z_{2})). It follows that the first factor Φi​(z1)\Phi_{i}(z_{1}) belongs to the corresponding semi-infinite plane and the same analysis shows that it has the form z1−j​(1+O⁡(z1))z_{1}^{-j}(1+O(z_{1})) as required. ∎

3.6. x−yx-y duality for dual points in the Sato–Wilson Grassmannian

The results of Corollary 3.16 can be further extended without an assumption on the triviality of the dual side in terms of the so-called dual points on the Sato–Wilson Grassmannian. It is merely a different point of view on Theorem 3.13.

Along with the kernel 𝕂⁡(z1,z2)\mathbb{K}(z_{1},z_{2}) consider also the dual kernel 𝕂∗​(z1,z2)=−𝕂⁡(z2,z1)\mathbb{K}^{*}(z_{1},z_{2})=-\mathbb{K}(z_{2},z_{1}). In the expansion at a regular point oo in the local coordinate zz it corresponds to the dual tau function Z∗​(p1,p2,…)=Z⁡(−p1,−p2,…)Z^{*}(p_{1},p_{2},\dots)=Z(-p_{1},-p_{2},\dots). Expanding this kernel in z2z_{2} we get

(3.22) −𝕂⁡(z2,z1)=𝕂∗​(z1,z2)=∑i=1∞Φi∗​(z1)​Φ1−i​(z2)​d​z1​d​z2,-\mathbb{K}(z_{2},z_{1})=\mathbb{K}^{*}(z_{1},z_{2})=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\Phi^{*}_{i}(z_{1})\Phi_{1-i}(z_{2})\sqrt{dz_{1}dz_{2}},

where the functions Φi∗\Phi^{*}_{i}, i≥1i\geq 1 generate a basis in the semi-infinite plane corresponding to the tau function Z∗Z^{*} and Φ1−i\Phi_{1-i}, i≥1i\geq 1, is the orthogonal dual basis in the space of regular power series. Remark that the choices of bases for the expansions (3.17) and (3.22) are independent. But for any choices we get a basis Φi\Phi_{i}, i∈ℤi\in\mathbb{Z} in the space of Laurent series in zz and the orthogonal dual in the sense of (3.18) basis Φi∗\Phi_{i}^{*}, i∈ℤi\in\mathbb{Z}, both satisfying Φi​(z)=z−i​(1+O⁡(z))\Phi_{i}(z)=z^{-i}(1+O(z)), Φi∗​(z)=z−i​(1+O⁡(z))\Phi_{i}^{*}(z)=z^{-i}(1+O(z)).

With this notation, the transformation rule for the Baker–Akhiezer kernel given in Theorem 3.13 has the following corollary.

Corollary 3.17.

Assume x′​y′x^{\prime}y^{\prime} has a pole of degree ≥3\geq 3 at z=0z=0. Let Φi∗,∨​(z)\Phi_{i}^{*,\vee}(z), i≥1i\geq 1 have the form z−i​(1+O​(z))z^{-i}(1+O(z)) and generate the semi-infinite plane corresponding to the tau function Z∗,∨​(p1,p2,…)=Z∨​(−p1,−p2,…)Z^{*,\vee}(p_{1},p_{2},\dots)=Z^{\vee}(-p_{1},-p_{2},\dots) where Z∨Z^{\vee} is x−yx-y dual to the tau function Z=Zo,zZ=Z_{o,z}. Then the following vectors Φi\Phi_{i}, i≥1i\geq 1, have the form Φi​(z)=z−i​(1+O⁡(z))\Phi_{i}(z)=z^{-i}(1+O(z)) and generate the semi-infinite plane corresponding to the tau function ZZ:

(3.23) Φi​(z)\displaystyle\Phi_{i}(z) =−x′​(z)2​π​ℏ​∫Φi∗,∨​(χ)​y′​(χ)​e1ℏ​(x⁡(z)​(y⁡(z)−y⁡(χ))+∫zχx​𝑑y)​𝑑χ,\displaystyle=\sqrt{\tfrac{-x^{\prime}(z)}{2\pi\hbar}}\int\Phi_{i}^{*,\vee}(\chi)\;\sqrt{{y^{\prime}(\chi)}}\;e^{\frac{1}{\hbar}\big(x(z)(y(z)-y(\chi))+\int_{z}^{\chi}xdy\big)}d\chi, i≥1.\displaystyle i\geq 1.
Proof.

We proceed in the same way as in the proof of Corollary 3.16. Using an expansion (3.22) for the x−yx-y dual kernel, we expand the left hand side of Equation (3.14) as

(3.24) 𝕂⁡(z1,z2)d​z1​d​z2\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{K}(z_{1},z_{2})}{\sqrt{dz_{1}dz_{2}}} =−x′​(z1)​x′​(z2)2​π​ℏ∬(∑i=1∞Φi∗,∨(χ2)Φ1−i∨(χ1))y′(χ1)y′(χ2)dχ1dχ2×\displaystyle=\tfrac{\sqrt{-x^{\prime}(z_{1})x^{\prime}(z_{2})}}{2\pi\hbar}\iint\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\Phi^{*,\vee}_{i}(\chi_{2})\Phi^{\vee}_{1-i}(\chi_{1})\Bigr)y^{\prime}(\chi_{1})y^{\prime}(\chi_{2})\,d\chi_{1}d\chi_{2}\times
e−1ℏ​(x⁡(z2)​(y⁡(z2)−y⁡(χ1))+∫z2χ1x​𝑑y)​e1ℏ​(x⁡(z1)​(y⁡(z1)−y⁡(χ2))+∫z1χ2x​𝑑y)\displaystyle\hskip 85.35826pte^{-\frac{1}{\hbar}\big(x(z_{2})(y(z_{2})-y(\chi_{1}))+\int_{z_{2}}^{\chi_{1}}xdy\big)}e^{\frac{1}{\hbar}\big(x(z_{1})(y(z_{1})-y(\chi_{2}))+\int_{z_{1}}^{\chi_{2}}xdy\big)}
=∑i=1∞Φi​(z1)​Φ1−i∗​(z2),\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\Phi_{i}(z_{1})\Phi^{*}_{1-i}(z_{2}),

where Φi\Phi_{i} is given by (3.23) and

The condition on the order of pole of x′​y′x^{\prime}y^{\prime} at z=0z=0 implies that Φi\Phi_{i} and Φ1−i∗\Phi^{*}_{1-i} have the form z1−i​(1+O⁡(z1))z_{1}^{-i}(1+O(z_{1})) and z2i−1​(1+O⁡(z2))z_{2}^{i-1}(1+O(z_{2})), respectively, and hence, this expansion of the kernel 𝕂\mathbb{K} provides a basis in the corresponding semi-infinite plane. ∎

Remark 3.18.

In the context of the path integral solutions to Douglas equation one considers the so-called p−qp-q duality, which describes a relation between two minimal models coupled to two-dimensional topological gravity, see [KM95]. In our language it should correspond to the swap of xx and yy defined to be polynomials of fixed finite degrees pp and qq, respectively. We claim that in these special cases the statements of Corollary 3.17 provide the p−qp-q duality proposed in [KM95], cf. Equation (27) in op. cit.

3.7. Topological recursion with non-ramified yy

A typical source of situations covered by Corollaries 3.16 and 3.15 comes from the theory of topological recursion. Assume Σ=ℂ​P1\Sigma=\mathbb{C}P^{1}, zz is a global coordinate on ℂ​P1\mathbb{C}P^{1}, and y⁡(z)=(a​z+b)/(c​z+d)y(z)=(az+b)/(cz+d) with a​d−b​c≠0ad-bc\neq 0. Under some conditions on xx and yy the theory of topological recursion assigns to this input a system of differentials {ωn(g)}\{\omega^{(g)}_{n}\}. These differentials are regular at the points o∈ℂ​P1o\in\mathbb{C}P^{1} where d​x≠0dx\not=0.

Theorem 3.19.

Let {ωn(g)}\{\omega^{(g)}_{n}\} be a system of differentials constructed by topological recursion for the input consisting of Σ=ℂ​P1\Sigma=\mathbb{C}P^{1} with a global coordinate zz and y⁡(z)=(a​z+b)/(c​z+d)y(z)=(az+b)/(cz+d). Let z=0z=0 be a regular point for the system of differentials. Then Z0,zZ_{0,z} is a KP tau function. Moreover, if x′​y′x^{\prime}y^{\prime} has a pole of degree at least 33 at z=0z=0, then the tau function Z0,zZ_{0,z} is described by the point of the semi-infinite Grassmannian spanned by Φi\Phi_{i}’s given by Equation (3.19).

Proof.

For such yy’s the x−yx-y swap relation can in fact replace topological recursion under an extra assumption that xx is a rational function and all zeros of d​xdx are simple. In this situation the x−yx-y swap relation actually provides us with explicit closed formulas for the system of differentials, see [ABDBKS25, Section 7].

In the case when not all zeros of d​xdx are simple one has to consider the so-called Bouchard–Eynard version of topological recursion, see [BE13], in combination with possibly having the pole of yy at a zero of d​xdx, cf. [CN19]. One can embed these cases in the families of functions xϵx_{\epsilon} such that the given xx is equal to x0x_{0} and for ϵ≠0\epsilon\not=0 all zeros of d​xϵdx_{\epsilon} are simple.

In this situation topological recursion is compatible with taking the limit ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0 [BBCKS23, Theorem 5.8], and the x−yx-y formula is compatible with the limit ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0 by construction. This allows us to wave the assumption that all zeros of d​xdx are simple and still apply Corollary 3.16. ∎

As a corollary of this theorem, we obtain the following explicit formulas in two important sets of examples (in these examples the limit procedure on the side of topological recursion is described in detail and proved in [CCGFG24, CGFG23]).

Corollary 3.20.

(1) Let x=z−r/rx=z^{-r}/r, y=−z−1y=-z^{-1}, r≥2r\geq 2. In this case the associated partition function Z0,zZ_{0,z} is known to be the string solution of the rr-th Gelfand–Dickey hierarchy. The corresponding point on the semi-infinite Grassmannian is given by

(3.26) Φi​(z)=12​π​ℏ​zr+1​∫χ−i−1​e1r⁡(r+1)​ℏ​(z−r−r​z−r−1​(χ−z)−χ−r)​𝑑χ,i≥1.\Phi_{i}(z)=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\hbar z^{r+1}}}\int\chi^{-i-1}e^{\frac{1}{r\,(r+1)\,\hbar}\big(z^{-r}-rz^{-r-1}(\chi-z)-\chi^{-r}\big)}d\chi,\qquad i\geq 1.

(2) Let x=z−r/rx=z^{-r}/r, y=−zy=-z, r≥2r\geq 2. It is the case of higher BGW discussed in Theorem 2.9. The corresponding point on the semi-infinite Grassmannian is given by

(3.27) Φi​(z)=i2​π​ℏ​zr+1​∫χ−i​e1r⁡(r−1)​ℏ​(−z1−r+(r−1)​z−r​(χ−z)+χ1−r)​𝑑χ,i≥1.\Phi_{i}(z)=\tfrac{\mathrm{i}}{\sqrt{2\pi\hbar z^{r+1}}}\int\chi^{-i}e^{\frac{1}{r\,(r-1)\,\hbar}\big(-z^{1-r}+(r-1)z^{-r}(\chi-z)+\chi^{1-r}\big)}d\chi,\qquad i\geq 1.

Theorem 2.9 is essentially a reformulation of the part (2)(2) of Corollary 3.20.

Proof of Theorem 2.9.

Indeed, up to the difference of conventions, expression describing the point (3.27) of the semi-infinite Grassmannian coincides with the expression of the point of Grassmannian for the higher Brézin–Gross–Witten tau function, given by [AD25, Equation (4.7)]. More specifically, to get the description [AD25] one should consider the inverse parameter z−1z^{-1} instead of zz and then divide (3.27) by zz. It remains to note that (3.27) uniquely specify the tau function, therefore it is given by the matrix integral (2.12). ∎

Corollary 3.20 can be immediately extended to the case where x=P⁡(z−1)x=P(z^{-1}) with arbitrary polynomial PP. In particular, if we take x=z−r/r−ϵ​z−1x=z^{-r}/r-\epsilon z^{-1} and y=−zy=-z with r≥2r\geq 2, then the set of the differentials constructed with topological recursion describes intersection numbers with the deformed rr-theta class [CGFG23, Theorem D]. We conclude that these differentials are KP integrable, moreover, the KP tau function Z0,zZ_{0,z} is associated with the point of the Grassmannian, generated by (3.19) with these xx and yy, that is

(3.28) Φi​(z)=−z−r−1+ϵ​z−22​π​ℏ​∫χ−i​e1ℏ​(1r⁡(r−1)​(−z1−r+(r−1)​z−r​(χ−z)+χ1−r)+ϵ⁡(1−χ/z+log⁡(χ/z)))​𝑑χ.\Phi_{i}(z)=\sqrt{\tfrac{-z^{-r-1}+\epsilon z^{-2}}{2\pi\hbar}}\int\chi^{-i}e^{\frac{1}{\hbar}\left(\frac{1}{r\,(r-1)}\left(-z^{1-r}+(r-1)z^{-r}(\chi-z)+\chi^{1-r}\right)+\epsilon\left(1-\chi/z+\log\left(\chi/z\right)\right)\right)}d\chi.

Note that this deformation coincides with the generalized higher BGW tau function, considered in [AD25, Section 5]. Indeed, if we consider it as a deformation of the spectral curve from Theorem 2.9, namely x=zr/r−ϵ​zx=z^{r}/r-\epsilon z, y=z−1y=z^{-1}, then this spectral curve can be described as r​yr−1​(x​y+ϵ)=1ry^{r-1}(xy+\epsilon)=1, which coincides with the spectral curve suggested in [AD25, Section 5] for the generalized higher BGW tau function if one identifies r=m+1r=m+1 and ϵ=S\epsilon=S. Moreover, the tau function Z∞,η−1Z_{\infty,\eta^{-1}} for η=(zr−ϵ​r​z)1/r\eta=(z^{r}-\epsilon rz)^{1/r} coincides, up to a (0,1)(0,1) contribution, with the generalized higher BGW tau function. The proof is based on the identification of the points of Grassmannian and is a direct generalization of proof of Theorem 2.9 where one should carefully treat the change of local coordinate.

Remark 3.21.

If y⁡(z)y(z) is linear fractional, then the triviality of the dual topological recursion follows from the fact that d​ydy has no zeros. However, there are other cases when the dual topological recursion is trivial and Corollary 3.16 is applied. It might happen that d​ydy gets zero at some point but d​xdx has a high order pole at the same point so that this point does not contribute to the poles of the dual topological recursion. For example, for the spectral curve

(3.29) x=zr,y=z−s,r>s>0,x=z^{r},\quad y=z^{-s},\quad r>s>0,

the Bouchard–Eynard version of topological recursion often makes no sense. But one can consider the x−yx-y swap relation as a properly replacement for topological recursion, which produces KP integrable differentials since the x−yx-y dual differentials are trivial. These tau functions should describe interesting enumerative geometry invariants, cf. [CGFG23] and [BKS24, Section 7].

Remark 3.22.

It would be interesting to compare the second statement of Corollary 3.20 (and its immediate extensions for arbitrary polynomials x=P⁡(z−1)x=P(z^{-1})) with the recently announced results of Shuai Guo, Ce Ji, and Qingsheng Zhang. In their talk “On a generalization of Witten’s conjecture through spectral curves” at the conference “Integrable systems and their applications” hold in Sochi, September 11-15, 2023, Shuai Guo asserted that in these cases they proved constrained KP integrability of the corresponding tau functions. At the moment of the present revision a preliminary version of their paper is available at [GJZ23].

4. Introduction, part 3: the structure of the x−yx-y swap relation

The goal of this section is to go deeper into the structure of x−yx-y swap relation between two systems of differentials, {ωn(g)}\{\omega^{(g)}_{n}\} and {ωn∨,(g)}\{\omega^{\vee,(g)}_{n}\}, without any reference to integrability (and only at the very end of this section we explain what its results mean in connection to KP integrability). In particular, we present in this section an (extended) reformulation of the x−yx-y swap relation which does not involve the complicated combinatorics of the sums over graphs of the original formulation.

The only assumptions that we have at the moment are the ones we made in Section 2.1.

The arrows in this diagram are certain transformations defined by explicit relations presented below and producing the object at the head of the arrow from the corresponding object on the tail. The main statement of this section claims that this diagram is commutative. It means that we can use transformations represented by some of the arrows as the definitions of the corresponding objects and then the remaining arrows represent universal functional identities. Remark that the identities implied by the left square in this diagram are actually treated in [ABDBKS25] under slightly different notations, while the identities implied by the right square of the diagram is an essential novelty of the present paper. The definitions of all involved objects is going to be ad hoc initially, but then they will be justified by the way they clarify the internal structure of Equation (2.8) and by the role they play in the KP integrable case. So let us introduce all objects and arrows in this diagram.

First of all we have:

(4.2) 𝕎n(g)=𝕎n(g)​(z⟦n⟧,u⟦n⟧)≔[ℏ2​g]⁡∏i=1ne−ui(𝒮(uiℏ∂xi)−1)yiui​∑Γℏ2​g​(Γ)|Aut⁡(Γ)|∏e∈E⁡(Γ)∏j=1|e|⌊(u~j,x~j)→(ue⁡(j),xe⁡(j))u~j𝒮(u~jℏ∂x~j)∑g~=0∞ℏ2​g~​ω~|e|(g~)​(z~⟦|e|⟧)∏j=1|e|d​x~j.\mathbb{W}^{(g)}_{n}=\mathbb{W}^{(g)}_{n}(z_{\llbracket n\rrbracket},u_{\llbracket n\rrbracket})\coloneqq\mathop{[{\hbar}^{2g}]}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{e^{-u_{i}(\mathcal{S}(u_{i}\hbar\partial_{x_{i}})-1)y_{i}}}{u_{i}}\sum_{\Gamma}\frac{\hbar^{2g(\Gamma)}}{|\mathrm{Aut}(\Gamma)|}\\ \prod_{e\in E(\Gamma)}\prod_{j=1}^{|e|}\mathop{\big\lfloor_{{(\tilde{u}_{j},\tilde{x}_{j})}\to{(u_{e(j)},x_{e(j)})}}}\tilde{u}_{j}\mathcal{S}(\tilde{u}_{j}\hbar\partial_{\tilde{x}_{j}})\sum_{\tilde{g}=0}^{\infty}\frac{\hbar^{2\tilde{g}}\tilde{\omega}^{(\tilde{g})}_{|e|}(\tilde{z}_{\llbracket|e|\rrbracket})}{\prod_{j=1}^{|e|}{d\tilde{x}_{j}}}.

Here as usual xi=x⁡(zi)x_{i}=x(z_{i}), x~i=x⁡(z~i)\tilde{x}_{i}=x(\tilde{z}_{i}), and yi=y⁡(zi)y_{i}=y(z_{i}). The sum is taken over all connected graphs Γ\Gamma with nn labeled vertices and multiedges of index ≥1\geq 1 with the same reservations as in (2.8). In particular, we exclude the contribution of (0,1)(0,1) edges in the graphs — this contribution is accounted in the first factor of the formula and it corresponds to the convention ω1(0)=−y​d​x\omega^{(0)}_{1}=-y\,dx. The functions 𝕎n(g)\mathbb{W}^{(g)}_{n} are symmetric functions in nn pairs of variables (zi,ui)(z_{i},u_{i}). We regard ziz_{i} as a point of the iith factor in Σn\Sigma^{n} while uiu_{i} is just a formal parameter. With the exception of 𝕎1(0)=1u1\mathbb{W}^{(0)}_{1}=\frac{1}{u_{1}} corresponding to leading term of the trivial graph, 𝕎n(g)\mathbb{W}^{(g)}_{n} is a polynomial in u1,…,unu_{1},\dots,u_{n} whose coefficients are meromorphic functions on Σn\Sigma^{n} represented as finite symbolic expressions in ωn(g)\omega^{(g)}_{n}’s, x′x^{\prime} and y′y^{\prime}.

We use exactly the same definition in the x−yx-y dual case, with the roles of xx and yy interchanged:

(4.3) 𝕎n∨,(g)=𝕎n∨,(g)​(z⟦n⟧,v⟦n⟧)≔[ℏ2​g]⁡∏i=1ne−vi(𝒮(viℏ∂yi)−1)xivi​∑Γℏ2​g​(Γ)|Aut⁡(Γ)|∏e∈E⁡(Γ)∏j=1|e|⌊(v~j,y~j)→(ve⁡(j),ye⁡(j))v~j𝒮(ℏ~vj∂y~j)∑g~=0∞ℏ2​g~​ω~|e|∨,(g~)​(z~⟦|e|⟧)∏j=1|e|d​y~j.\mathbb{W}^{\vee,(g)}_{n}=\mathbb{W}^{\vee,(g)}_{n}(z_{\llbracket n\rrbracket},v_{\llbracket n\rrbracket})\coloneqq\mathop{[{\hbar}^{2g}]}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{e^{-v_{i}(\mathcal{S}(v_{i}\hbar\partial_{y_{i}})-1)x_{i}}}{v_{i}}\sum_{\Gamma}\frac{\hbar^{2g(\Gamma)}}{|\mathrm{Aut}(\Gamma)|}\\ \prod_{e\in E(\Gamma)}\prod_{j=1}^{|e|}\mathop{\big\lfloor_{{(\tilde{v}_{j},\tilde{y}_{j})}\to{(v_{e(j)},y_{e(j)})}}}\tilde{v}_{j}\mathcal{S}(\tilde{\hbar}v_{j}\partial_{\tilde{y}_{j}})\sum_{\tilde{g}=0}^{\infty}\frac{\hbar^{2\tilde{g}}\tilde{\omega}^{\vee,(\tilde{g})}_{|e|}(\tilde{z}_{\llbracket|e|\rrbracket})}{\prod_{j=1}^{|e|}{d\tilde{y}_{j}}}.

In a similar way, we define

(4.4) Ωn=Ωn​(w⟦n⟧,w¯⟦n⟧)≔∏i=1n1xi−x¯i​∑Γ1|Aut⁡(Γ)|∏e∈E⁡(Γ)∏j=1|e|⌊(w~j,w¯~j)→(we⁡(j),w¯e⁡(j))∫w¯~1w~1∫w¯~2w~2⋯∫w¯~|e|w~|e|∑g~=0∞ℏ2​g~−2+|e|ω~(g~)|e|(z~⟦|e|⟧)\Omega_{n}=\Omega_{n}(w_{\llbracket n\rrbracket},\bar{w}_{\llbracket n\rrbracket})\coloneqq\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{x_{i}-\bar{x}_{i}}\sum_{\Gamma}\frac{1}{|\mathrm{Aut}(\Gamma)|}\\ \prod_{e\in E(\Gamma)}\prod_{j=1}^{|e|}\mathop{\big\lfloor_{{(\tilde{w}_{j},\tilde{\bar{w}}_{j})}\to{(w_{e(j)},\bar{w}_{e(j)})}}}\int_{\tilde{\bar{w}}_{1}}^{\tilde{w}_{1}}\!\!\!\int_{\tilde{\bar{w}}_{2}}^{\tilde{w}_{2}}\!\!\!\!\cdots\!\!\int_{\tilde{\bar{w}}_{|e|}}^{\tilde{w}_{|e|}}\sum_{\tilde{g}=0}^{\infty}\hbar^{2\tilde{g}-2+|e|}\tilde{\omega}^{(\tilde{g})}_{|e|}(\tilde{z}_{\llbracket|e|\rrbracket})

and

(4.5) Ωn∨=Ωn∨​(w⟦n⟧,w¯⟦n⟧)≔∏i=1n1yi−y¯i​∑Γ1|Aut⁡(Γ)|∏e∈E⁡(Γ)∏j=1|e|⌊(w~j,w¯~j)→(we⁡(j),w¯e⁡(j))∫w¯~1w~1∫w¯~2w~2⋯∫w¯~|e|w~|e|∑g~=0∞ℏ2​g~−2+|e|ω~∨,(g~)|e|(z~⟦|e|⟧).\Omega^{\vee}_{n}=\Omega^{\vee}_{n}(w_{\llbracket n\rrbracket},\bar{w}_{\llbracket n\rrbracket})\coloneqq\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{y_{i}-\bar{y}_{i}}\sum_{\Gamma}\frac{1}{|\mathrm{Aut}(\Gamma)|}\\ \prod_{e\in E(\Gamma)}\prod_{j=1}^{|e|}\mathop{\big\lfloor_{{(\tilde{w}_{j},\tilde{\bar{w}}_{j})}\to{(w_{e(j)},\bar{w}_{e(j)})}}}\int_{\tilde{\bar{w}}_{1}}^{\tilde{w}_{1}}\!\!\!\int_{\tilde{\bar{w}}_{2}}^{\tilde{w}_{2}}\!\!\!\!\cdots\!\!\int_{\tilde{\bar{w}}_{|e|}}^{\tilde{w}_{|e|}}\sum_{\tilde{g}=0}^{\infty}\hbar^{2\tilde{g}-2+|e|}\tilde{\omega}^{\vee,(\tilde{g})}_{|e|}(\tilde{z}_{\llbracket|e|\rrbracket}).

These are the functions on Σ2​n\Sigma^{2n} defined in the neighborhoods of the product of diagonals in Σ2\Sigma^{2} corresponding to the pairs of variables (wi,w¯i)(w_{i},\bar{w}_{i}).

Comparing the definitions of 𝕎n(g)\mathbb{W}^{(g)}_{n} and Ωn\Omega_{n} we see that 𝕎n(g)\mathbb{W}^{(g)}_{n} can be obtained from Ωn\Omega_{n} by the substitution wi=eℏ​ui2∂xiziw_{i}=e^{\frac{\hbar u_{i}}{2}\partial_{x_{i}}}z_{i}, w¯i=e−ℏ​ui2∂xizi\bar{w}_{i}=e^{-\frac{\hbar u_{i}}{2}\partial_{x_{i}}}z_{i} with an additional account of (0,1)(0,1) contribution. Remark 4.1.

The substitution wi=eℏ​ui2∂xiziw_{i}=e^{\frac{\hbar u_{i}}{2}\partial_{x_{i}}}z_{i}, w¯i=e−ℏ​ui2∂xizi\bar{w}_{i}=e^{-\frac{\hbar u_{i}}{2}\partial_{x_{i}}}z_{i} means that the arguments (zi,ui)(z_{i},u_{i}) of the function 𝕎n(g)\mathbb{W}^{(g)}_{n} represent a point in a neighborhood of the diagonal in Σ2\Sigma^{2}, and the substitution provides a parametrization of this neighborhood.

Notice that for 2​g−2+n≥02g-2+n\geq 0 we have
