Remark 4.2.

Relations (4.9) and (4.10) suggest that a more invariant version of the functions 𝕎n(g)\mathbb{W}^{(g)}_{n}, 𝕎n∨,(g)\mathbb{W}^{\vee,(g)}_{n}, Ωn\Omega_{n}, Ωn∨\Omega^{\vee}_{n} would be the differentials 𝕎n(g)​∏i=1nd​xi\mathbb{W}^{(g)}_{n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}dx_{i}, 𝕎n∨,(g)​∏i=1nd​yi\mathbb{W}^{\vee,(g)}_{n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}dy_{i} and half-differentials Ωn​∏i=1nd​xi​d​x¯i\Omega_{n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\sqrt{dx_{i}d\bar{x}_{i}}, Ωn∨​∏i=1nd​yi​d​y¯i\Omega^{\vee}_{n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\sqrt{dy_{i}d\bar{y}_{i}}, respectively. However, in order to keep the exposition more explicit we prefer to deal with functions rather than with (half)differentials.

4.2. Extended x−yx-y swap relations

It proves out that there are equations relating the functions 𝕎ng\mathbb{W}^{g}_{n} and 𝕎n∨,(g)\mathbb{W}^{\vee,(g)}_{n}, or, respectively, Ωn\Omega_{n} and Ωn∨\Omega^{\vee}_{n} directly, avoiding complicated combinatorics of summation over graphs. These equations form the missing part of Diagram (4.1):
Theorem 4.3.

The x−yx-y swap relations admit the following extensions:

(4.18) 𝕎n(g)​(z⟦n⟧,u⟦n⟧)\displaystyle\mathbb{W}^{(g)}_{n}(z_{\llbracket n\rrbracket},u_{\llbracket n\rrbracket}) =(−1)n​∏i=1n(eui​yi​∑ri=0∞∂xiri[viri]​d​yid​xi​e−ui​yi)​𝕎n∨,(g)​(z⟦n⟧,v⟦n⟧),\displaystyle=(-1)^{n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\bigg(e^{u_{i}y_{i}}\sum_{r_{i}=0}^{\infty}\partial_{x_{i}}^{r_{i}}[v_{i}^{r_{i}}]\frac{dy_{i}}{dx_{i}}e^{-u_{i}y_{i}}\bigg)\mathbb{W}^{\vee,(g)}_{n}(z_{\llbracket n\rrbracket},v_{\llbracket n\rrbracket}),
(4.19) 𝕎n∨,(g)​(z⟦n⟧,v⟦n⟧)\displaystyle\mathbb{W}^{\vee,(g)}_{n}(z_{\llbracket n\rrbracket},v_{\llbracket n\rrbracket}) =(−1)n​∏i=1n(evi​xi​∑ri=0∞∂yiri[uiri]​d​xid​yi​e−vi​xi)​𝕎n(g)​(z⟦n⟧,u⟦n⟧),\displaystyle=(-1)^{n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\bigg(e^{v_{i}x_{i}}\sum_{r_{i}=0}^{\infty}\partial_{y_{i}}^{r_{i}}[u_{i}^{r_{i}}]\frac{dx_{i}}{dy_{i}}e^{-v_{i}x_{i}}\bigg)\mathbb{W}^{(g)}_{n}(z_{\llbracket n\rrbracket},u_{\llbracket n\rrbracket}),
(4.20) Ωn​(w⟦n⟧,w¯⟦n⟧)\displaystyle\Omega_{n}(w_{\llbracket n\rrbracket},\bar{w}_{\llbracket n\rrbracket}) =(−i2​π​ℏ)n∫⋯∫Ωn∨(χ⟦n⟧,χ¯⟦n⟧)∏i=1ny′(χi)y′(χ¯i)∏i=1ndχidχ¯i×\displaystyle=\Bigl(\frac{-\mathrm{i}}{2\pi\hbar}\Bigr)^{n}\int\!\!\cdots\!\!\!\int\Omega^{\vee}_{n}(\chi_{\llbracket n\rrbracket},\bar{\chi}_{\llbracket n\rrbracket})\prod_{i=1}^{n}y^{\prime}(\chi_{i})y^{\prime}(\bar{\chi}_{i})\prod_{i=1}^{n}d\chi_{i}d\bar{\chi}_{i}\times
∏i=1neOPEN−1ℏ​(x⁡(w¯i))​(y⁡(w¯i)−y⁡(χi))+∫w¯iχix​𝑑y)​e1ℏ​(x⁡(wi)​(y⁡(wi)−y⁡(χ¯i))+∫wiχ¯ix​𝑑y),\displaystyle\qquad\prod_{i=1}^{n}e^{-\frac{1}{\hbar}\big(x(\bar{w}_{i}))(y(\bar{w}_{i})-y(\chi_{i}))+\int_{\bar{w}_{i}}^{\chi_{i}}xdy\big)}e^{\frac{1}{\hbar}\big(x(w_{i})(y(w_{i})-y(\bar{\chi}_{i}))+\int_{w_{i}}^{\bar{\chi}_{i}}xdy\big)},
(4.21) Ωn∨​(w⟦n⟧,w¯⟦n⟧)\displaystyle\Omega^{\vee}_{n}(w_{\llbracket n\rrbracket},\bar{w}_{\llbracket n\rrbracket}) =(−i2​π​ℏ)n∫⋯∫Ωn(χ⟦n⟧,χ¯⟦n⟧)∏i=1nx′(χi)x′(χ¯i)∏i=1ndχidχ¯i×\displaystyle=\Bigl(\frac{-\mathrm{i}}{2\pi\hbar}\Bigr)^{n}\int\!\!\cdots\!\!\!\int\Omega_{n}(\chi_{\llbracket n\rrbracket},\bar{\chi}_{\llbracket n\rrbracket})\prod_{i=1}^{n}{x^{\prime}(\chi_{i})x^{\prime}(\bar{\chi}_{i})}\prod_{i=1}^{n}d\chi_{i}d\bar{\chi}_{i}\times
∏i=1neOPEN−1ℏ​(y⁡(w¯i))​(x⁡(w¯i)−x⁡(χi))+∫w¯iχiy​𝑑x)​e1ℏ​(y⁡(wi)​(x⁡(wi)−x⁡(χ¯i))+∫wiχ¯iy​𝑑x),\displaystyle\qquad\prod_{i=1}^{n}e^{-\frac{1}{\hbar}\big(y(\bar{w}_{i}))(x(\bar{w}_{i})-x(\chi_{i}))+\int_{\bar{w}_{i}}^{\chi_{i}}ydx\big)}e^{\frac{1}{\hbar}\big(y(w_{i})(x(w_{i})-x(\bar{\chi}_{i}))+\int_{w_{i}}^{\bar{\chi}_{i}}ydx\big)},

where the formal Gaussian integrals are understood in the same way as in Theorem 3.13.

The first two relations of this theorem concerning the functions 𝕎n(g)\mathbb{W}^{(g)}_{n} and 𝕎n∨,(g)\mathbb{W}^{\vee,(g)}_{n} are proved in a bit different formulation in [ABDBKS25]. An extended reference to the op. cit. and a proof of the other two relations is given in Section 7 below.

Proof of Theorem 3.13.

This theorem is a direct corollary of Theorem 4.3. Indeed, by construction, Ω1​(w,w¯)=K⁡(w,w¯)\Omega_{1}(w,\bar{w})=K(w,\bar{w}) and Ω1∨​(w,w¯)=K∨​(w,w¯)\Omega^{\vee}_{1}(w,\bar{w})=K^{\vee}(w,\bar{w}). ∎

4.3. Extended determinantal formulas

We want to stress that in the whole Section 4 up to this point and in particular in Theorem 4.3 we don’t use any assumption on integrability. Meanwhile, in the KP integrable case some of the relations admit simplification. Namely, we have the following strengthening of Theorem 2.8.

Theorem 4.4.

Assume that the system of differentials {ωn(g)}\{\omega^{(g)}_{n}\} is KP integrable in the sense of Theorem 2.3. Then the functions Ωn\Omega_{n} and the x−yx-y dual functions Ωn∨\Omega^{\vee}_{n} admit determinantal presentations

(4.22) Ωn​(w⟦n⟧,w¯⟦n⟧)\displaystyle\Omega_{n}(w_{\llbracket n\rrbracket},\bar{w}_{\llbracket n\rrbracket}) =(−1)n−1​∑σ∈Cn∏i=1nK⁡(wi,w¯σ⁡(i)),\displaystyle=(-1)^{n-1}\sum_{\sigma\in C_{n}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}K(w_{i},\bar{w}_{\sigma(i)}), n≥1,\displaystyle n\geq 1,
(4.23) Ωn∨​(w⟦n⟧,w¯⟦n⟧)\displaystyle\Omega^{\vee}_{n}(w_{\llbracket n\rrbracket},\bar{w}_{\llbracket n\rrbracket}) =(−1)n−1​∑σ∈Cn∏i=1nK∨​(wi,w¯σ⁡(i)),\displaystyle=(-1)^{n-1}\sum_{\sigma\in C_{n}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}K^{\vee}(w_{i},\bar{w}_{\sigma(i)}), n≥1,\displaystyle n\geq 1,

where K⁡(w,w¯)=𝕂⁡(w,w¯)d​x​(w)​d​x​(w¯)K(w,\bar{w})=\frac{\mathbb{K}(w,\bar{w})}{\sqrt{dx(w)\,dx(\bar{w})}} and K∨​(w,w¯)=𝕂∨​(w,w¯)d​y​(w)​d​y​(w¯)K^{\vee}(w,\bar{w})=\frac{\mathbb{K}^{\vee}(w,\bar{w})}{\sqrt{dy(w)\,dy(\bar{w})}} are the same as in Theorem 3.13.

Proof.

For the first equality we should use computations in the Fock space and apply Wick formula, the same as for the proof of (3.3). To this end, we just observe that in a local expansion in the KP integrable case we can compute the connected correlation functions associated with the following expression

(4.24) ⟨0|​∏i=1n(∑li∈ℤψli​w¯i−li−1​∑ri∈ℤψri∗​wiri)​v\displaystyle\langle 0|\prod_{i=1}^{n}\bigg(\sum_{l_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}}\psi_{l_{i}}\bar{w}_{i}^{-l_{i}-1}\sum_{r_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}}\psi^{*}_{r_{i}}w_{i}^{r_{i}}\bigg)v

(here vv is the corresponding decomposable vector as in (2.2)) in two different ways. The first way is to rewrite each factor ∑li∈ℤψli​w¯i−li−1​∑ri∈ℤψri∗​wiri\sum_{l_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}}\psi_{l_{i}}\bar{w}_{i}^{-l_{i}-1}\sum_{r_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}}\psi^{*}_{r_{i}}w_{i}^{r_{i}} as a bosonic operator and use the argument in [BDBKS22, Section 3 and 4], which gives the left hand side of (4.22). On the other hand, one can compute (4.24) using the Wick formula, and this gives the right hand side of (4.22).

Now to prove (4.23) we will use Theorem 4.3. Substitute the right hand side of (4.22) to (4.21). Then the determinant expression in the right hand side of (4.22) allows to apply the x−yx-y duality transformation for KK from Theorem 3.13, and finally we obtain exactly (4.23).

∎

Now we are ready to prove one of the main results of the paper, using Theorem 4.3, which we prove in Section 7.

Proof of Theorem 2.8.

If {ωn(g)}\{\omega^{(g)}_{n}\} is KP integrable then we have (4.22) and hence (4.23). Restricting to the product of diagonals wi=w¯iw_{i}=\bar{w}_{i} we establish the validity of the determinantal formulas for the x−yx-y dual differentials {ωn∨(g)}\{\omega^{\vee(g)}_{n}\}, which implies, in turn, their KP integrability. ∎

Part II Details and proofs

5. Semi-classical limit equation and implications

In this Section we prove Proposition 3.6 in a bit more technical but convenient formulation. Recall that the KP integrability property for a system of differentials can be reformulated as a system of equations (3.7) and (3.8) on these differentials. In particular, let us consider the leading term in ℏ\hbar of (3.7) for n=2n=2:

(5.1) ω2(0)=e∫x2x1∫x2x1(ω2(0)−ω2(0)​sing)​ω2(0)​sing,\displaystyle{\omega^{(0)}_{2}}=e^{\int\limits_{x_{2}}^{x_{1}}\int\limits_{x_{2}}^{x_{1}}(\omega^{(0)}_{2}-\omega^{(0)\rm sing}_{2})}{\omega^{(0)\rm sing}_{2}},

where

(5.2) ω2(0)​sing=d​x1​d​x2(x1−x2)2.\omega^{(0)\rm sing}_{2}=\frac{dx_{1}dx_{2}}{(x_{1}-x_{2})^{2}}.

This equality can be considered as an equation on the unknown bidifferential ω2(0)\omega^{(0)}_{2}. Proposition 3.6 is obtained by solving this equation. Namely, we reformulate Proposition 3.6 in the following more explicit form.

Lemma 5.1.

Consider a bi-differential ω2(0)\omega^{(0)}_{2} on Σ2\Sigma^{2}, which has a double pole on the diagonal with bi-residue 11. Assume that o∈Σo\in\Sigma is a regular point for ω2(0)\omega^{(0)}_{2}. Let xx be a local coordinate at oo. Then all solutions of Equation (5.1) are given by

(5.3) ω2(0)=d​z1​d​z2(z1−z2)2,zi=z⁡(xi),\omega^{(0)}_{2}=\frac{dz_{1}dz_{2}}{(z_{1}-z_{2})^{2}},\quad z_{i}=z(x_{i}),

where z⁡(x)z(x) is certain Laurent series at oo that extends as a global meromorphic function zz on Σ\Sigma.

For a given ω2(0)\omega^{(0)}_{2} that resolves Equation (5.1) the corresponding function zz is defined uniquely up to a linear fractional transformation.

Proof.

At the first step of the proof we are going to solve this equation in the space of formal symmetric power expansions in x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} (as it is done in [TT95, Proposition B.2]). In fact, it follows from (3.10) that the equation of Lemma is independent of the choice of local coordinate xx. This implies immediately that any bidifferential of the form (5.3) does satisfy this equation. So, for the first step of the argument it is sufficient to show that (5.1) has no solutions other than those of the form (5.3).

Moreover, since Equation (5.1) is invariant with respect to a change of local coordinate, we can choose the local coordinate in any convenient way such that the given solution ω2(0)\omega^{(0)}_{2} takes as simple form as possible. Denote by α\alpha the 11-form obtained from ω2(0)\omega^{(0)}_{2} by specifying any nonzero tangent vector at the point o∈Σo\in\Sigma for the second argument in ω2(0)\omega^{(0)}_{2}. Then α\alpha has a pole of order 22 at oo with the trivial residue, and we can choose a local coordinate zz such that α=d​zz2\alpha=\frac{dz}{z^{2}}, that is,

(5.4) z=−(∫α)−1,z=-\Big(\int\alpha\Big)^{-1},

with an arbitrary choice of the integration constant. Then, for the expansion

(5.5) ω2(0)=d​z1​d​z2(z1−z2)2+d1​d2​H2(0),H2(0)=∑i,j=1∞ci,j​z1i​z2j,\omega^{(0)}_{2}=\frac{dz_{1}dz_{2}}{(z_{1}-z_{2})^{2}}+d_{1}d_{2}H^{(0)}_{2},\qquad H^{(0)}_{2}=\sum_{i,j=1}^{\infty}c_{i,j}z_{1}^{i}z_{2}^{j},

our choice of the local coordinate zz is equivalent to requirement c1,i=ci,1=0c_{1,i}=c_{i,1}=0 for all i≥1i\geq 1.

Let us solve (5.1) inductively by computing homogeneous terms of H2(0)H^{(0)}_{2} in (5.5) step by step. Denote by hd​(z1,z2)=∑i=1d−1ci,d−i​z1i​z2d−ih_{d}(z_{1},z_{2})=\sum_{i=1}^{d-1}c_{i,d-i}z_{1}^{i}z_{2}^{d-i} the degree dd term of H2(0)H^{(0)}_{2}. Then for hd​(z1,z2)h_{d}(z_{1},z_{2}) we obtain an equation of the following kind

(5.6) ∂2hd​(z1,z2)∂z1​∂z2−hd​(z1,z1)−hd​(z1,z2)−hd​(z2,z1)+hd​(z2,z2)(z1−z2)2=r.h.s.\frac{\partial^{2}h_{d}(z_{1},z_{2})}{\partial z_{1}\partial z_{2}}-\frac{h_{d}(z_{1},z_{1})-h_{d}(z_{1},z_{2})-h_{d}(z_{2},z_{1})+h_{d}(z_{2},z_{2})}{(z_{1}-z_{2})^{2}}=\text{r.h.s}.

where the right hand side is expressed in terms of the polynomials hd′h_{d^{\prime}} for d′<dd^{\prime}<d computed in the previous steps of the induction.

This equation implies a system of linear equations for ci,jc_{i,j}, i,j≥1i,j\geq 1, i+j=di+j=d. We are only interested in the solutions of this system of equations that satisfy c1,d−1=cd−1,1=0c_{1,d-1}=c_{d-1,1}=0 (as it is demanded by our choice of the coordinate zz) and is symmetric under the swap of indices, ci,j=cj,ic_{i,j}=c_{j,i}. In order to prove that there are no non-trivial solutions of this linear system that satisfy these properties let us consider the left hand side of (5.6) as an operator AdA_{d} acting in the vector space of degree d−2d-2 homogeneous symmetric polynomials in z1,z2z_{1},z_{2} and taking z1−1​z2−1​hd​(z1,z2)z_{1}^{-1}z_{2}^{-1}h_{d}(z_{1},z_{2}) to the left hand side of (5.6). It is easy to find explicitly the eigenbasis of AdA_{d}. Namely, it is checked by direct substitution that the polynomial vd,0=z1d−1−z2d−1z1−z2=∑i=0d−2z1i​z2d−2−iv_{d,0}=\frac{z_{1}^{d-1}-z_{2}^{d-1}}{z_{1}-z_{2}}=\sum_{i=0}^{d-2}z_{1}^{i}z_{2}^{d-2-i} is an eigenvector of AdA_{d} with the eigenvalue 00, and the following polynomial

(5.7) vd,i=(z1​z2)i−1​(z1j−z2jz1−z2−j2​(z1j−1+z2j−1)),j=d+1−2​i,v_{d,i}=(z_{1}z_{2})^{i-1}\Bigl(\frac{z_{1}^{j}-z_{2}^{j}}{z_{1}-z_{2}}-\frac{j}{2}(z_{1}^{j-1}+z_{2}^{j-1})\Bigr),\qquad j=d+1-2i,

is an eigenvector of AdA_{d} with the eigenvalue i⁡(d−i)i(d-i) for i=1,…,⌊d2⌋i=1,\dots,\lfloor\frac{d}{2}\rfloor. It follows that AdA_{d} has one-dimensional kernel spanned by vd,0v_{d,0} and it is non-degenerate on the span of the remaining eigenvectors consisting of symmetric polynomials vanishing on the diagonal z1=z2z_{1}=z_{2}.

Now we can return to the analysis of Equation (5.6). If we want to use it to determine hd​(z1,z2)h_{d}(z_{1},z_{2}) assuming that hd′≡0h_{d^{\prime}}\equiv 0 for d′<dd^{\prime}<d (which is trivially true for d′<2d^{\prime}<2), then we see from the above analysis of the structure of the operator AdA_{d} that the only non-trivial solution that we get is proportional to z1​z2​vd,0=∑i=1d−1z1i​z2d−iz_{1}z_{2}v_{d,0}=\sum_{i=1}^{d-1}z_{1}^{i}z_{2}^{d-i}. Since by our choice of the coordinate zz we have an additional assumption that the coefficients of z1​z2d−1z_{1}z_{2}^{d-1} and z1d−1​z2z_{1}^{d-1}z_{2} must be equal to zero, we conclude that hd​(z1,z2)h_{d}(z_{1},z_{2}) must be equal to zero as well. This holds for any d≥2d\geq 2. So, we conclude H2(0)=0H^{(0)}_{2}=0 and ω2(0)=d​z1​d​z2(z1−z2)\omega^{(0)}_{2}=\frac{dz_{1}dz_{2}}{(z_{1}-z_{2})} for the specified choice of the local coordinate, as claimed.

Remark 5.2.

Note that though we insisted above on a convenient choice of a coordinate zz near oo, we could also just derive the same change of variables perturbatively trivializing the coefficients of the zero eigenvectors of AdA_{d}, d≥2d\geq 2, in any coordinate. To this end just note that

(5.8) d⁡(z1+ϵ​z1d)​d​(z2+ϵ​z2d)(z1+ϵ​z1d−(z2+ϵ​z2d))2=d​z1​d​z2(z1−z2)2+ϵ​d1​d2​∑i=1d−1z1i​z2d−i+O⁡(ϵ).\frac{d(z_{1}+\epsilon z_{1}^{d})d(z_{2}+\epsilon z_{2}^{d})}{(z_{1}+\epsilon z_{1}^{d}-(z_{2}+\epsilon z_{2}^{d}))^{2}}=\frac{dz_{1}dz_{2}}{(z_{1}-z_{2})^{2}}+\epsilon d_{1}d_{2}\sum_{i=1}^{d-1}z_{1}^{i}z_{2}^{d-i}+O(\epsilon).

Note, however, in our approach we defined zz as an actual local coordinate near o∈Σo\in\Sigma, not just as a formal power series in xx, so we obtained a stronger statement than we initially intended to do at the first step of the proof.

So, we obtained that the equality (5.3) holds in a suitably defined local coordinate zz in a neighborhood of the point (o,o)∈Σ2(o,o)\in\Sigma^{2}. At the second step of the proof we want to show that the introduced local coordinate zz extends as a global meromorphic function, which would imply that (5.3) extends as an equality of globally defined meromorphic bidifferentials on Σ\Sigma.

By construction, there exists an open neighborhood o∈U⊆Σo\in U\subseteq\Sigma such that zz is a local coordinate on UU and

(5.9) ω2(0)|U×U=d​z1​d​z2(z1−z2)2.\omega^{(0)}_{2}|_{U\times U}=\frac{dz_{1}dz_{2}}{(z_{1}-z_{2})^{2}}.

The local coordinate zz is defined up to a fractional linear transformation z→a​z/(c​z+d)z\to az/(cz+d), a,c,d∈ℂa,c,d\in\mathbb{C}, a​d≠0ad\not=0 (it is the effect of the choices of tangent vector and integration constant hidden in (5.4)). From the fact that ω2(0)\omega^{(0)}_{2} is globally defined it follows that d​z/z2dz/z^{2} extends to a global meromorphic form on Σ\Sigma.

Applying the same construction of a convenient local coordinate to any other point o′∈Uo^{\prime}\in U and using Equation (5.9) for ω2(0)\omega^{(0)}_{2} on U×UU\times U, we obtain that for each fractional linear transformation w=(a​z+b)/(c​z+d)w=(az+b)/(cz+d), a,b,c,d∈ℂa,b,c,d\in\mathbb{C}, a​d−b​c≠0ad-bc\not=0, w(o′)=0⇔z(o′)=−b/aw(o^{\prime})=0\Leftrightarrow z(o^{\prime})=-b/a, that is, −b/a-b/a is sufficiently close to 00, we still have that d​w/w2dw/w^{2} extends to a global meromorphic form on Σ\Sigma.

So, not only d​z/z2dz/z^{2} extends to a globally defined meromorphic form on Σ\Sigma, but any fractional linear transformation of zz sufficiently close to identity does the same. It is a very strong property that is sufficient to derive that zz is a global meromorphic function itself. Indeed, it means in particular that

(5.10) d​z(z−t)2\frac{dz}{(z-t)^{2}}

is a global defined meromorphic form for any tt small enough, hence

(5.11) d​zz2d​z(z−t)2=(1−t​z−1)2\frac{\frac{dz}{z^{2}}}{\frac{dz}{(z-t)^{2}}}=(1-tz^{-1})^{2}

is a globally defined meromorphic function for any tt small enough. It is a polynomial in tt, so the coefficients of tt and t2t^{2} are globally defined meromorphic functions. Hence, z−1z^{-1} (the coefficient of tt) and, therefore, zz are globally defined meromorphic functions. Lemma 5.1 and Proposition 3.6 are proved. ∎

6. Computations with Gaussian integrals

6.1. A formal Gaussian integral

By a Gaussian integral we mean an expression of the form

(6.1) ∫…​∫P⁡(ξ1,…,ξn)​e−Q⁡(ξ1,…,ξn)​d​ξ1​…​d​ξn,\int\!\!\dots\!\!\int P(\xi_{1},\dots,\xi_{n})e^{-Q(\xi_{1},\dots,\xi_{n})}d\xi_{1}\dots d\xi_{n},

where QQ is a nondegenerate quadratic form and PP is a polynomial, or a power series in auxiliary variable ℏ\sqrt{\hbar} with polynomial coefficients. We treat Gaussian integrals formally, one can think of them using the following computational rules merely as definitions:

(6.2) 12​π​∫ξk​e−a​ξ22​𝑑ξ≔{0,k=1,3,5,…,(k−1)!!​a−k+12,k=0,2,4,…;\displaystyle\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int\xi^{k}e^{-a\frac{\xi^{2}}{2}}d\xi\coloneqq\begin{cases}0,&k=1,3,5,\dots,\\ (k-1)!!a^{-\frac{k+1}{2}},&k=0,2,4,\dots;\end{cases}
(6.3) i2​π​∬ξk​ζℓ​e−ξ​ζ​𝑑ξ​𝑑ζ≔δk​ℓ​k!,\displaystyle\tfrac{\mathrm{i}}{{2\pi}}\iint\xi^{k}\zeta^{\ell}e^{-\xi\zeta}d\xi d\zeta\coloneqq\delta_{k\ell}k!,

here (−1)!!=1(-1)!!=1. In all computations below one can think of a suitable choice of contours that makes this formulas work, and the terms of this shape appear in the formal ℏ\sqrt{\hbar} expansion.

The main tool in dealing with a formal Gaussian integral is its invariance under a change of variables. The allowed changes should consist of a linear invertible transformation plus a series in positive powers of ℏ\sqrt{\hbar} with polynomial coefficients. For example, Equation (6.3) can be recovered from (6.2) by a linear transform reducing the quadratic function −ξ​ζ-\xi\zeta to a diagonal form and reducing thereby a multiple integral to a repeated one.

Remark 6.1.

Note that each change of variables in the Gaussian integral make sense only once one performs the corresponding re-parametrization of the integration cycle (or rather the local germ of the integration cycle near the critical point), with the proper choice of orientation. In order to keep the computations below readable, we decided to omit the discussion of the integration cycles in the computations; it is rather straightforward to reconstruct them at each step.

In order to illustrate how a typical computation with the Gaussian integrals works, let us explain the meaning of the integral (3.12),

(6.4) f⁡(z)=i2​π​ℏ​∫f∨​(χ)​y′​(χ)​e1ℏ​(x⁡(z)​(y⁡(z)−y⁡(χ))+∫zχx​𝑑y)​𝑑χ.f(z)=\tfrac{\mathrm{i}}{\sqrt{2\pi\,\hbar}}\int f^{\vee}(\chi)\;y^{\prime}(\chi)\;e^{\frac{1}{\hbar}\left(x(z)(y(z)-y(\chi))+\int_{z}^{\chi}x\,dy\right)}\,d\chi.

Applying the Taylor expansion of the exponent at the point χ=z\chi=z we compute

(6.5) 1ℏ​(x⁡(z)​(y⁡(z)−y⁡(χ))+∫zχx​y′​𝑑z)=12​x′​(z)​y′​(z)​(χ−z)2ℏ+O⁡((χ−z)3).\tfrac{1}{\hbar}\Bigl(x(z)(y(z)-y(\chi))+\int_{z}^{\chi}x\,y^{\prime}\,dz\Bigr)=\frac{1}{2}x^{\prime}(z)y^{\prime}(z)\tfrac{(\chi-z)^{2}}{\hbar}+O((\chi-z)^{3}).

This expression is a quadratic form in ξ=χ−zℏ\xi=\tfrac{\chi-z}{\sqrt{\hbar}} plus higher order corrections involving positive powers of ℏ\sqrt{\hbar}. Therefore, applying the shift χ=z+ℏ​ξ\chi=z{+}\sqrt{\hbar}\xi we can rewrite this integral as

(6.6) f⁡(z)=i2​π​∫f∨​(z+ℏ​ξ)​y′​(z+ℏ​ξ)​e∑k≥2ℏk2−1​ak​(z)​ξkk!​𝑑ξ,f(z)=\tfrac{\mathrm{i}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int f^{\vee}(z{+}\sqrt{\hbar}\,\xi)\;y^{\prime}(z{+}\sqrt{\hbar}\,\xi)\;e^{\sum_{k\geq 2}\hbar^{\frac{k}{2}-1}a_{k}(z)\frac{\xi^{k}}{k!}}d\xi,

where

(6.7) ak​(z)≔∂zk−1(x​y′)−x​y(k).a_{k}(z)\coloneqq\partial_{z}^{k-1}(xy^{\prime})-xy^{(k)}.

The summand in the exponent with k=2k=2 is quadratic in ξ\xi and the higher order terms contain positive powers of ℏ\sqrt{\hbar}. Thus, the obtained integral takes a standard form of Gaussian integral and can be computed in the expansion in ℏ\sqrt{\hbar} using the rule (6.2) with a=−x′​(z)​y′​(z)a=-x^{\prime}(z)y^{\prime}(z). In fact, the coefficients of the half-integer powers of ℏ\hbar involve odd powers of ξ\xi only and do not contribute to the integral. As a result, f⁡(z)f(z) is a series in nonnegative integer powers of ℏ\hbar whose coefficients are certain rational combinations of derivatives of different order of the functions f∨f^{\vee}, xx, yy and a common factor y′/x′\sqrt{y^{\prime}/x^{\prime}}:

(6.8) f⁡(z)=y′x′​(f∨+(f∨​x(3)8​(x′)2​y′−f∨​y(3)8​x′​(y′)2−5​f∨​(x′′)224​(x′)3​y′+f∨​x′′​y′′24​(x′)2​(y′)2+f∨​(y′′)26​x′​(y′)3+f∨⁣′​x′′2​(x′)2​y′−f∨′′2​x′​y′)​ℏ+O⁡(ℏ2)).f(z)=\frac{\sqrt{y^{\prime}}}{\sqrt{x^{\prime}}}\Bigl(f^{\vee}+\bigl(\tfrac{f^{\vee}x^{(3)}}{8(x^{\prime})^{2}y^{\prime}}-\tfrac{f^{\vee}y^{(3)}}{8x^{\prime}(y^{\prime})^{2}}-\tfrac{5f^{\vee}(x^{\prime\prime})^{2}}{24(x^{\prime})^{3}y^{\prime}}+\tfrac{f^{\vee}x^{\prime\prime}y^{\prime\prime}}{24(x^{\prime})^{2}(y^{\prime})^{2}}+\tfrac{f^{\vee}(y^{\prime\prime})^{2}}{6x^{\prime}(y^{\prime})^{3}}+\tfrac{f^{\vee\prime}x^{\prime\prime}}{2(x^{\prime})^{2}y^{\prime}}-\tfrac{f^{\vee\prime\prime}}{2x^{\prime}y^{\prime}}\bigr)\hbar+O(\hbar^{2})\Bigr).
Remark 6.2.

From (6.6) we see that the integral transform sending f∨f^{\vee} to ff depends on x′​(z)x^{\prime}(z) and y′​(z)y^{\prime}(z) only, or, equivalently, on d​xdx and d​ydy.

This transform acts pointwise in a sense that the value of ff at the point zz depends on the values of f∨f^{\vee} in a vicinity of the point zz only. The value f⁡(z)f(z) is not always defined at zeros and poles of d​xdx and d​ydy, and in the complement to these points the coefficient of each particular power of ℏ\hbar of this transform acts as a finite order differential operator with holomorphic coefficients.

To be precise, Equation (6.2) shows that ff involves negative half-integer powers of x′x^{\prime} and y′y^{\prime}. In other words, for any rational exponents aa and bb the function f∨​(x′)a​(y′)bf^{\vee}(x^{\prime})^{a}(y^{\prime})^{b} is globally meromorphic if and only if f​(x′)a+1/2​(y′)b+1/2f(x^{\prime})^{a+1/2}(y^{\prime})^{b+1/2} is globally meromorphic on Σ\Sigma.

Let us now apply a change of variables from the local coordinate χ\chi to the local coordinate ϕ\phi defined by an implicit equation

(6.9) y⁡(χ)=y⁡(z)+ℏ​ϕ.y(\chi)=y(z)+\sqrt{\hbar}\phi.

More explicitly, this change is given by χ=eϕℏ∂yz\chi=e^{\phi\sqrt{\hbar}\partial_{y}}z and its action on any function gg is given by g(χ)=eϕℏ∂yg(z)g(\chi)=e^{\phi\sqrt{\hbar}\partial_{y}}g(z). With this change the integral (6.4) takes the following form

(6.10) f⁡(z)\displaystyle f(z) =i2​π∫f∨(χ)e∑k≥2ℏk2−1​∂yk−1x​ϕkk!dϕ,f∨(χ)=eϕℏ∂yf∨(z).\displaystyle=\tfrac{\mathrm{i}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int f^{\vee}(\chi)\;e^{\sum_{k\geq 2}\hbar^{\frac{k}{2}-1}\partial_{y}^{k-1}x\frac{\phi^{k}}{k!}}d\phi,\qquad f^{\vee}(\chi)=e^{\phi\sqrt{\hbar}\partial_{y}}f^{\vee}(z).

Here we again use the Taylor expansion of the function g⁡(χ)=∫zχx​𝑑yg(\chi)=\int\limits_{z}^{\chi}xdy. The term in the exponent with k=2k=2 is quadratic in ϕ\phi and the higher order terms involve positive powers of ℏ\hbar. Therefore, we obtained a standard form of a Gaussian integral (6.2) with a=−d​xd​ya=-\frac{dx}{dy}.

Alternatively, we can use another coordinate ψ\psi given by

(6.11) x⁡(χ)=x⁡(z)+ℏ​ψ,x(\chi)=x(z)+\sqrt{\hbar}\psi,

and we compute for this coordinate applying integration by parts in the exponent

(6.12) f⁡(z)\displaystyle f(z) =i2​π​∫f∨​(χ)​y′​(χ)​eOPEN−1ℏ​((x⁡(z)−x⁡(χ))​y​(χ))+∫zχy​𝑑x)​𝑑χ\displaystyle=\tfrac{\mathrm{i}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int f^{\vee}(\chi)\;y^{\prime}(\chi)\;e^{-\frac{1}{\hbar}\left((x(z)-x(\chi))y(\chi))+\int_{z}^{\chi}y\,dx\right)}\,d\chi
=i2​π​∫f∨​(χ)​y′​(χ)x′​(χ)​e∑k≥2ℏk2−1​(k−1)​∂xk−1y​ψkk!​dψ,\displaystyle=\tfrac{\mathrm{i}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int f^{\vee}(\chi)\;\frac{y^{\prime}(\chi)}{x^{\prime}(\chi)}\;e^{\sum_{k\geq 2}\hbar^{\frac{k}{2}-1}(k-1)\partial_{x}^{k-1}y\frac{\psi^{k}}{k!}}d\psi,
f∨​(χ)​y′​(χ)x′​(χ)\displaystyle f^{\vee}(\chi)\;\frac{y^{\prime}(\chi)}{x^{\prime}(\chi)} =eψℏ∂x(f∨(z)y′​(z)x′​(z)).\displaystyle=e^{\psi\sqrt{\hbar}\partial_{x}}\Bigl(f^{\vee}(z)\;\frac{y^{\prime}(z)}{x^{\prime}(z)}\Bigr).

Equivalence of (6.6), (6.10), and (6.12) follows from invariance of Gaussian integrals under the changes. Note that (6.10) shows, in particular, that the transformation sending f∨f^{\vee} to ff is independent of the choice of the coordinate zz.

In a similar way, the Gaussian integral realizing the inverse transformation (3.13) can be represented in either of the following equivalent forms

6.2. Key identity

The main tool relating different forms of x−yx-y duality transformation is contained in the following identity.

Lemma 6.3.

Let y=y⁡(z)y=y(z) be a meromorphic function and g⁡(z,u)g(z,u) be a series in ℏ\hbar whose coefficients are meromorphic functions on the spectral curve depending on an additional parameter uu in a polynomial way. Assume that g⁡(z,u/ℏ)g(z,u/\sqrt{\hbar}) involves non-negative powers of ℏ\hbar only. Then the following identity holds

(6.16) ∑r≥0∂yr[ur]​g​(z,u)=i2​π​∬g⁡(ζ,u)​y′​(ζ)​e−u⁡(y⁡(ζ)−y⁡(z))​𝑑u​𝑑ζ.\sum_{r\geq 0}\partial_{y}^{r}[u^{r}]g(z,u)=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi}\iint g(\zeta,u)\,y^{\prime}(\zeta)\,e^{-u\,(y(\zeta)-y(z))}du\,d\zeta.

The double integral on the right hand side is understood in the sense of asymptotic expansion at small absolute value of ℏ\hbar at ζ=z\zeta=z.

Proof.

Using (6.3) we compute:

(6.17) ∑r≥0∂yr\displaystyle\sum_{r\geq 0}\partial_{y}^{r} [ur]​g​(z,u)=∑r≥0ℏr/2​∂yr[ur]​g​(z,u/ℏ)\displaystyle[u^{r}]g(z,u)=\sum_{r\geq 0}\hbar^{r/2}\partial_{y}^{r}[u^{r}]g(z,u/\sqrt{\hbar})
=∑r≥0ℏr/2​∂yri2​π​∬vrr!​g​(z,u/ℏ)​e−u​v​𝑑u​𝑑v\displaystyle=\sum_{r\geq 0}\hbar^{r/2}\partial_{y}^{r}\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi}\iint\frac{v^{r}}{r!}g(z,u/\sqrt{\hbar})\,e^{-u\,v}du\,dv
=i2​π∬evℏ∂yg(z,u/ℏ)e−u​vdudv.\displaystyle=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi}\iint e^{v\sqrt{\hbar}\partial_{y}}g(z,u/\sqrt{\hbar})\,e^{-u\,v}du\,dv.
=i2​π​∬g⁡(ζ,u/ℏ)​e−u​v​𝑑u​𝑑v\displaystyle=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi}\iint g(\zeta,u/\sqrt{\hbar})\,e^{-u\,v}du\,dv
=i2​π​∬g⁡(ζ,u)​e−u​ℏ​v​du​ℏ​dv.\displaystyle=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi}\iint g(\zeta,u)\,e^{-u\,\sqrt{\hbar}v}du\,\sqrt{\hbar}dv.

where ζ=ζ(z,v)=evℏ∂yz\zeta=\zeta(z,v)=e^{v\sqrt{\hbar}\partial_{y}}z. Let us consider an expression for ζ\zeta in terms of vv as a change of variables in the integral. Equivalently, this change is determined by an implicit equation y⁡(ζ)=y⁡(z)+v​ℏy(\zeta)=y(z)+v\sqrt{\hbar} implying that y′​(ζ)​d​ζ=ℏ​d​vy^{\prime}(\zeta)d\zeta=\sqrt{\hbar}\,dv. The obtained integral expression written in coordinates uu and ζ\zeta takes the form exactly as in Lemma. ∎

Remark 6.4.

A rescaling of the parameter uu involving non-integer powers of ℏ\hbar is needed for the change of variables in the Gaussian integral to make sense. Recall that an allowed change involves a linear invertible transformation plus a series in positive powers of ℏ\hbar with polynomial coefficients. In that sense, the actual variables of integration in the integral (6.16) for which this integral takes a standard form (6.1) of a formal Gaussian integral are (ℏ​u,ζ−zℏ)\bigl(\sqrt{\hbar}\,u,\frac{\zeta-z}{\sqrt{\hbar}}\bigr)

Therefore, in order to prove commutativity of this square it is sufficient to prove commutativity of the corresponding transformations for one particular index. The commutativity of this reduced set of transformations acting on functions in just two variables is checked in this section.

The transformations forming Diagram (6.3) commute.

Remark 6.6.

To make sense to the computations in the proof, we imply that all involved variables are regarded with certain scales. In order to da that the integrals involved take the standard form (6.1) of formal Gaussian integral on each step of computations. For example, for the integrals (6.22) and (6.23) we assume that χ−w¯ℏ=O⁡(ℏ0)\frac{\chi-\bar{w}}{\sqrt{\hbar}}=O(\hbar^{0}), χ¯−wℏ=O⁡(ℏ0)\frac{\bar{\chi}-w}{\sqrt{\hbar}}=O(\hbar^{0}). For the integral (6.28) we assume u​ℏ=O⁡(ℏ0)u\sqrt{\hbar}=O(\hbar^{0}), ζ−zℏ=O⁡(ℏ0)\frac{\zeta-z}{\sqrt{\hbar}}=O(\hbar^{0}). With these scales all the changes have allowed form of a linear transform plus terms of positive order in ℏ\hbar with polynomial coefficients.
